stem: A company streams clickstream events into an Amazon Kinesis data stream that has 8 shards. Three consumer applications read the stream. After the third application was added, all three began receiving ReadProvisionedThroughputExceeded errors and fell behind. The company must give each application dedicated read throughput of 2 MB/s per shard and must reduce propagation delay to approximately 70 ms. The company cannot change the shard count. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Increase the stream from 8 shards to 24 shards to provide more aggregate read throughput.
Configure each application to call GetRecords less frequently with a larger batch size.
Register each application as an enhanced fan-out consumer and read records with SubscribeToShard.
Replace the stream with an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream.

explanation: C is correct. Enhanced fan-out gives every registered consumer a dedicated 2 MB/s per shard pipe and pushes records over HTTP/2 with about 70 ms of propagation delay, without changing the shard count. A is wrong because the 2 MB/s read limit is per shard and shared by all standard consumers, and the company cannot change the shard count. B is wrong because polling less often increases propagation delay rather than reducing it to 70 ms, and read throughput stays shared. D is wrong because Firehose buffers before delivery, so latency is seconds or minutes, and a delivery stream is not a source that multiple consumer applications subscribe to.

stem: An AWS Glue Spark job reads 500,000 small JSON objects each day from Amazon S3 and writes Apache Parquet output. The job runs for four hours on 20 G.1X workers, spends most of that time in the read stage, and shows low executor CPU usage. Each run also reprocesses every object that has ever landed in the source prefix. Which two actions will reduce the job's runtime and cost? (Choose two.)

options.text: Change the job type from Apache Spark to Python shell to run on a single 1 DPU worker.
Enable AWS Glue job bookmarks so that each run processes only the objects that arrived since the last run.
Increase the number of G.1X workers from 20 to 80 to run more read tasks in parallel.
Enable input file grouping so that each Spark task reads a group of many small objects.
Write the output as gzip-compressed .csv instead of Apache Parquet to shrink the output objects.

explanation: B is correct because job bookmarks persist state between runs, so each run reads only new objects, which cuts both runtime and DPU hours. D is correct because low CPU usage with one task per object is the small files problem; grouping many objects into each task removes per-task overhead on the same workers. A is wrong because a Python shell job has no Spark cluster and cannot distribute 500,000 objects, so it would run far longer and cost more. C is wrong because it holds DPU hours roughly constant while the small-file overhead remains, so it does not reduce cost. E is wrong because it does not touch the read stage where the time is spent, and gzip .csv is neither columnar nor splittable, which slows downstream queries.

stem: A company stores 300 TB of event data as Hive-style partitioned Apache Parquet files in Amazon S3 and queries the data with Amazon Athena and Amazon EMR. Privacy rules now require the company to delete individual customers' rows on request, which currently means rewriting whole partitions. Auditors also need to query the table as it existed at an earlier time. The data must stay in Amazon S3. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning and S3 Object Lock on the bucket. Have auditors read previous object versions.
Extend the AWS Glue job to rewrite each affected partition. Copy partitions to a dated backup prefix.
Load the data into an Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster. Run DELETE statements and take a snapshot before each load.
Convert the tables to Apache Iceberg tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Use Athena DELETE and time travel queries.

explanation: D is correct. Iceberg adds a metadata layer over the existing Parquet files that supports row-level DELETE and snapshot-based time travel, and both Athena and Amazon EMR read Iceberg tables cataloged in AWS Glue, so the data stays in Amazon S3. A is wrong because object versions give no table-level consistent snapshot to query, and Object Lock prevents the deletions the privacy rules require. B is wrong because it keeps the whole-partition rewrite the company wants to eliminate and substitutes manual backup copies for snapshots. C is wrong because it moves the data out of Amazon S3, and a cluster snapshot restores an entire cluster rather than letting auditors query one table as of a past time.

stem: A company stores 20 million product embeddings of 1,024 dimensions in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition cluster that uses the pgvector extension. A semantic search API must return the top 20 nearest neighbors in under 50 ms with the highest possible recall. The instance has ample memory, and the catalog is rebuilt overnight, so a long index build is acceptable. Which indexing approach will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an IVFFlat index that uses a small number of lists.
Create no index and rely on an exact sequential scan for perfect recall.
Create a B-tree index on the embedding column for ORDER BY.
Create an HNSW index and accept its longer build time and memory use.

explanation: D is correct. HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph that gives the best recall-versus-latency tradeoff of the pgvector index types, and its costs are slower builds and higher memory, both of which this workload tolerates. A is wrong because IVFFlat trades recall for speed, and a small number of lists makes each list large, so probing one is slow while recall still trails HNSW. B is wrong because an exact scan of 20 million high-dimension vectors reads the whole table on every query and cannot return results in under 50 ms. C is wrong because a B-tree orders scalar values and has no notion of vector distance, so PostgreSQL cannot use it for an approximate nearest-neighbor search.

stem: A company queries five years of application logs with Amazon Athena. The logs are in Amazon S3 under a predictable year, month, day, and hour prefix layout that has produced about 44,000 partitions. An AWS Glue crawler runs hourly to register new partitions and now takes 40 minutes. Analysts report long query planning times. The company must reduce planning time and stop paying for partition registration. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Run MSCK REPAIR TABLE on an hourly schedule with Amazon EventBridge. Delete the AWS Glue crawler.
Rewrite the data as one unpartitioned table that is bucketed on the event timestamp column.
Run the AWS Glue crawler every five minutes against only the newest prefix in the bucket.
Enable partition projection on the table by defining ranges for the partition keys. Delete the crawler.

explanation: D is correct. Partition projection lets Athena compute partition values from configured ranges instead of listing 44,000 partitions in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, which removes the planning-time lookup and makes partition registration unnecessary. A is wrong because MSCK REPAIR TABLE still writes every partition into the catalog, so planning stays slow, and a full repair over 44,000 partitions is itself expensive. B is wrong because removing partitions forces Athena to scan far more data for a single-day query, and bucketing does not prune by date. C is wrong because running the crawler more often increases cost instead of eliminating it and does nothing about planning time.

stem: A nightly Apache Spark job on Amazon EMR joins a 4 TB transactions dataset to a 200 GB merchants dataset on merchant_id. The job now runs for six hours. In the Spark UI, 199 of the join stage's 200 tasks finish within two minutes, but one task processes 40 times more shuffle data and spills to disk. One merchant accounts for most of the transactions. Which solution will reduce the runtime?

options.text: Increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions from 200 to 2000 to spread the shuffle across more tasks.
Cache the transactions DataFrame with the MEMORY_AND_DISK storage level before the join.
Enable adaptive query execution skew join handling and add a salt value to the join key.
Broadcast the 4 TB transactions dataset so that the join runs as a broadcast hash join.

explanation: C is correct. One task with 40 times the shuffle data is key skew: adaptive query execution splits skewed partitions at runtime, and salting spreads the hot merchant's rows across several partitions so no single task dominates. A is wrong because hash partitioning sends every row with the same merchant_id to one partition no matter how many partitions exist, so the hot key stays in one oversized task. B is wrong because the problem is the distribution of shuffle data, not repeated source reads, and caching 4 TB consumes the memory the skewed task needs. D is wrong because a broadcast side must fit in each executor's memory, so broadcasting 4 TB fails; the merchants side is the broadcast candidate.

stem: A company's data account holds a customers table in a data lake that is registered with AWS Lake Formation. An analytics team in another AWS account must query the table with Amazon Athena. The team must not see the ssn or salary columns and must not see rows for customers outside the EU. The company must not duplicate the data. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a Lake Formation data filter that omits the two columns and limits rows to the EU. Grant the analytics account SELECT with the filter.
Create an Athena view over the permitted columns and rows. Add a bucket policy that lets the analytics account read the underlying objects.
Run an AWS Glue job that writes a filtered copy of the table to a second bucket. Share that bucket with the analytics account.
Ask the analytics account administrator to attach an IAM policy that denies s3:GetObject on prefixes that hold non-EU customer data.

explanation: A is correct. A Lake Formation data filter expresses column exclusions and a row filter on one table, and a cross-account grant with that filter is enforced for every Athena query without copying the data. B is wrong because granting the analytics account direct read access to the objects lets analysts bypass the view and read the ssn and salary columns. C is wrong because it duplicates the dataset, which the requirements prohibit, and adds a second copy of regulated data to secure. D is wrong because S3 prefixes cannot express a column restriction, and row filtering by prefix works only if the data happens to be partitioned by region.

stem: A healthcare company lands partner files in an Amazon S3 raw zone. Some files contain PII in columns whose names differ by partner. The company must automatically discover which objects contain PII and which sensitive data types they hold. The curated datasets that analysts query with Amazon Athena must contain no readable PII. The company wants to avoid custom pattern-matching code. Which two actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery jobs on the raw zone bucket to find and classify PII.
Enable Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection to inspect uploaded objects and report PII findings.
Encrypt the curated bucket with an AWS KMS key and omit the analyst roles from the key policy.
Create an AWS Config rule that marks objects that contain PII as noncompliant.
Apply AWS Glue PII detection and redaction transforms in the job that writes the curated datasets.

explanation: A is correct because Macie uses managed data identifiers to find and classify sensitive data in Amazon S3 without custom regular expressions and reports the affected objects and data types. E is correct because the Glue PII detection and redaction transforms mask or hash the detected columns as the curated output is written, so analysts never see readable PII. B is wrong because GuardDuty S3 Protection analyzes CloudTrail data events for anomalous access and does not classify object contents. C is wrong because Athena decrypts objects with the caller's permissions, so excluding analysts from the key policy blocks the whole dataset instead of masking PII columns. D is wrong because AWS Config evaluates resource configurations rather than file contents, so it cannot detect PII inside objects.

stem: A data engineer configures an AWS Glue job to read data from an Amazon S3 bucket. The engineer has created the AWS Glue connection details and an associated IAM role that grants access to the bucket. When the engineer runs the job, the job fails with an error that indicates a problem with the Amazon S3 VPC gateway endpoint. Which solution will resolve the error?

options.text: Update the AWS Glue security group to allow inbound traffic from the Amazon S3 VPC gateway endpoint.
Configure an S3 bucket policy that explicitly grants the AWS Glue job permission to access the bucket.
Confirm that the AWS Glue connection details specify a fully qualified domain name for Amazon S3.
Verify that the route table for the job's subnets includes a route to the S3 VPC gateway endpoint.

explanation: D is correct. A gateway endpoint is reached through a route table entry that sends the Amazon S3 prefix list to the endpoint, so a subnet whose route table lacks that entry cannot reach Amazon S3 and the job fails. A is wrong because a gateway endpoint has no elastic network interface and no security group, and the Glue connection initiates outbound traffic rather than receiving inbound traffic. B is wrong because the failure is a network path problem, not an authorization problem; the IAM role already grants the required access. C is wrong because AWS Glue resolves the Amazon S3 endpoint through DNS automatically, and the connection details do not take a fully qualified domain name for Amazon S3.

stem: A retail company stores a customer data hub in an Amazon S3 bucket. Analysts in many countries use the hub for company-wide analytics. A governance team must ensure that each analyst can access data only for customers who are in the same country as the analyst. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Create a separate table for each country. Grant each analyst access to the table for the country the analyst serves.
Register the S3 bucket as a data lake location in AWS Lake Formation. Use Lake Formation row-level security to enforce the policy.
Move each country's data to an AWS Region near that country. Grant each analyst access to the Region that the analyst serves.
Load the data into Amazon Redshift. Create a view and an IAM role for each country. Assign the roles to the analysts.

explanation: B is correct. Lake Formation row-level security applies a row filter to a single registered table, so one policy set governs every analyst and no restructuring or copying of the data hub is needed. A is wrong because splitting the hub into one table per country multiplies the tables, pipelines, and grants that the governance team must maintain as countries are added. C is wrong because Region placement is a data residency and latency decision that does not enforce row-level access, and relocating data across Regions is a large migration effort. D is wrong because a view and an IAM role for each country is far more ongoing administration than a single row filter, and it requires loading the data into a new data store.

stem: A media company wants to improve a system that recommends content to customers based on user behavior and preferences. To improve the recommendations, the company must incorporate insights from third-party datasets into the company's existing analytics platform. The company wants to minimize the effort and time that are required to incorporate the third-party datasets. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Subscribe to the datasets in AWS Data Exchange. Use API calls to access and integrate the datasets.
Use AWS DataSync to transfer the third-party datasets. Use API calls to access and integrate them.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to access and integrate third-party datasets from Amazon ECR.
Use Amazon AppFlow to access and integrate third-party datasets from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store.

explanation: A is correct. AWS Data Exchange is the AWS marketplace for third-party data: the company subscribes to a product and the data is delivered into its own account through the Data Exchange APIs, with no ingestion pipeline to build or maintain. B is wrong because DataSync moves data between storage systems the company already has access to; it does not provide or license third-party datasets. C is wrong because Amazon ECR is a container image registry, not a source of third-party datasets, and Kinesis Data Streams cannot read from it. D is wrong because Parameter Store holds configuration values and secrets rather than datasets, so it is not a source that Amazon AppFlow would integrate for analytics.

stem: A financial company wants to implement a data mesh. The data mesh must support centralized data governance, data analysis, and data access control. The company has decided to use AWS Glue for data catalogs and for extract, transform, and load (ETL) operations. Which combination of AWS services will implement the data mesh? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use Amazon Aurora for data storage. Use an Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster for data analysis.
Use Amazon S3 for data storage. Use Amazon Athena for data analysis.
Use AWS Glue DataBrew for centralized data governance and access control.
Use Amazon RDS for data storage. Use Amazon EMR for data analysis.
Use AWS Lake Formation for centralized data governance and access control.

explanation: B is correct because a data mesh on AWS uses Amazon S3 as the shared storage layer that producer domains publish into, and Athena queries that storage directly through the AWS Glue Data Catalog. E is correct because Lake Formation is the service that provides the centralized permissions, cross-account sharing, and governance layer the data mesh requires. A is wrong because Aurora is a relational database for operational workloads rather than a shared data mesh storage layer, and a provisioned Redshift cluster centralizes analysis instead of federating it. C is wrong because DataBrew is a visual data preparation tool; it does not provide governance or access control. D is wrong because Amazon RDS is an operational database that is not a data mesh storage layer, and Amazon EMR alone supplies no governance or access control.

stem: A data engineer maintains custom Python scripts that perform a data formatting process that many AWS Lambda functions use. When the data engineer needs to modify the Python scripts, the data engineer must manually update all of the Lambda functions. The data engineer requires a less manual way to update the Lambda functions. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Store a pointer to the custom Python scripts in the execution context object.
Package the custom Python scripts into a Lambda layer. Apply the layer to the Lambda functions.
Store a pointer to the custom Python scripts in an environment variable of each Lambda function.
Assign the same alias to each Lambda function. Invoke each Lambda function by specifying the alias.

explanation: B is correct. A Lambda layer packages shared code once; publishing a new layer version and pointing the functions at it replaces per-function code updates with a single artifact update. A is wrong because the execution context is per-invocation runtime state, not a distribution mechanism, so it cannot deliver updated shared code to the functions. C is wrong because an environment variable holds a value, so each function would still need code to fetch and load the scripts, and every function's configuration would still need updating. D is wrong because an alias is a pointer to a version of one function and does not share code between functions.

stem: A company created an extract, transform, and load (ETL) data pipeline in AWS Glue. A data engineer must crawl a table that is in Microsoft SQL Server. The data engineer needs to extract, transform, and load the output of the crawl to an Amazon S3 bucket. The data engineer also must orchestrate the data pipeline. Which AWS service or feature will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: AWS Step Functions
AWS Glue workflows
AWS Glue Studio
Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA)

explanation: B is correct. Glue workflows orchestrate Glue crawlers and jobs natively and carry no additional charge beyond the crawler and job runs themselves, so the whole pipeline stays inside AWS Glue. A is wrong because Step Functions adds per-state-transition charges and an extra service to build and maintain for orchestration that AWS Glue already provides. C is wrong because Glue Studio is a visual authoring interface for Glue jobs, not an orchestration feature for sequencing a crawler and jobs. D is wrong because Amazon MWAA bills for a continuously running Airflow environment, which is the most expensive option for scheduling a single Glue pipeline.

stem: A financial services company stores financial data in Amazon Redshift. A data engineer wants to run real-time queries on the financial data to support a web-based trading application. The data engineer wants to run the queries from within the trading application without managing persistent database connections. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Establish WebSocket connections from the trading application to Amazon Redshift.
Call the Amazon Redshift Data API from the trading application.
Set up Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) connections to Amazon Redshift.
Copy frequently accessed data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to run the queries.

explanation: B is correct. The Redshift Data API is an HTTPS endpoint that runs SQL without a persistent connection or a driver, authenticates with IAM or Secrets Manager, and is designed for web applications to call directly. A is wrong because Amazon Redshift does not accept WebSocket connections, so the application cannot query the cluster this way. C is wrong because JDBC requires the application to manage a driver and a connection pool, which is exactly the persistent-connection overhead the engineer wants to avoid. D is wrong because copying data to Amazon S3 adds a pipeline and staleness, so queries no longer run against real-time data in Amazon Redshift.

stem: A company uses Amazon Athena for one-time queries against data that is in Amazon S3. The company has several use cases. The company must implement permission controls to separate query processes and access to query history among users, teams, and applications that are in the same AWS account. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an S3 bucket for each use case. Grant appropriate individual IAM users access through an S3 bucket policy.
Create an Athena workgroup for each use case. Apply tags to the workgroups and use tag conditions in an IAM policy.
Create an IAM role for each use case. Assign appropriate permissions to each role and associate the role with Athena.
Create an AWS Glue Data Catalog resource policy that grants individual IAM users access to the specific tables that Athena uses.

explanation: B is correct. Workgroups are the Athena construct that isolates query execution and query history, and tagging them lets one IAM policy grant each team access to only its own workgroup. A is wrong because bucket policies control access to the underlying data, not to Athena query execution or query history, which is what must be separated. C is wrong because roles alone grant permissions but provide no boundary around query history or query processing, and Athena has no role association of this kind. D is wrong because a Data Catalog resource policy governs metadata access to databases and tables and does not separate query history between teams.

stem: A data engineer needs to schedule a workflow that runs a set of AWS Glue jobs every day. The data engineer does not require the AWS Glue jobs to run or to finish at a specific time, and occasional delays are acceptable. Which solution will run the AWS Glue jobs in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Choose the FLEX execution class in the AWS Glue job properties.
Choose the Spot Instance type in the AWS Glue job properties.
Choose the STANDARD execution class in the AWS Glue job properties.
Choose the latest version in the GlueVersion field of the AWS Glue job properties.

explanation: A is correct. The FLEX execution class runs jobs on spare capacity at a lower price and is intended exactly for non-urgent jobs whose start and finish times can vary. B is wrong because AWS Glue is serverless and its job properties expose no Spot Instance type for the engineer to select. C is wrong because STANDARD is the higher-priced class that provides dedicated capacity and fast, predictable start times, which this workload does not need. D is wrong because the Glue version determines the Apache Spark and Python runtime, so it can affect performance but is not a pricing class.

stem: A data engineer needs to create an AWS Lambda function that converts the format of data from .csv to Apache Parquet. The Lambda function must run only if a user uploads a .csv file to an Amazon S3 bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an S3 event notification for the s3:ObjectCreated:* event type with a suffix filter rule for .csv. Set the Lambda function ARN as the destination.
Create an S3 event notification for the s3:ObjectTagging:* event type for objects that have a tag set to .csv. Set the Lambda function ARN as the destination.
Create an S3 event notification for the s3:* event type with a suffix filter rule for .csv. Set the Lambda function ARN as the destination.
Create an S3 event notification for s3:ObjectCreated:* with a suffix filter for .csv. Publish to an Amazon SNS topic that invokes the function.

explanation: A is correct. The s3:ObjectCreated:* event type fires on upload, the suffix filter restricts notifications to .csv objects, and a Lambda destination invokes the function directly with nothing else to operate. B is wrong because object tagging events fire when tags change rather than when a file is uploaded, so an upload would not trigger the function. C is wrong because s3:* includes deletion and restore events, so the function would run on operations other than uploads. D is wrong because inserting an SNS topic adds a component to configure, secure, and pay for without changing the outcome, so it carries more operational overhead than a direct destination.

stem: A gaming company stores player profile updates in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Five downstream applications must each process every item-level change, and the company must be able to reprocess changes from the past 5 days after an outage. The company currently uses DynamoDB Streams and reports that consumers are throttled and that older changes are unavailable. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Increase the provisioned read capacity of the DynamoDB table, and retry throttled stream reads with exponential backoff in each application.
Turn on Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB, and configure each application as a consumer of the stream.
Create a DynamoDB global table replica in a second Region, and read the replica's stream from each of the applications.
Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table, and have each application query a restored copy of the table every hour.

explanation: B is correct. Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB sends item-level change records to a Kinesis stream, which supports many more concurrent consumers than the two-per-shard limit of DynamoDB Streams and supports a retention period of up to 365 days, so 5 days of replay is available. A is wrong because read capacity units govern table reads, not stream reads; the throttling comes from the per-shard consumer limit of DynamoDB Streams, and the 24-hour stream retention still prevents 5-day replay. C is wrong because a global table replica has the same DynamoDB Streams limits, so it does not add consumer capacity or retention. D is wrong because point-in-time recovery produces full table restores, not an ordered feed of item-level changes, and hourly restores are slow and expensive.

stem: A retail company runs a self-managed PostgreSQL database on Amazon EC2. A data engineer must copy the existing tables to Amazon S3 and then keep the S3 data current as rows change in the database. The engineer must not write custom change-capture code. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an AWS DMS task that uses the full load only migration type, and schedule the task to run every hour.
Create an AWS DMS task that uses the full load and change data capture (CDC) migration type.
Configure the PostgreSQL source for logical replication, and grant the DMS user replication permissions.
Create an AWS Glue job that reads the tables through JDBC and overwrites the S3 objects every hour.
Create an Amazon AppFlow flow that uses the PostgreSQL database as the source and Amazon S3 as the target.

explanation: B is correct because the full load and CDC migration type first copies the existing rows and then continuously applies inserts, updates, and deletes to the Amazon S3 target with no custom code. C is correct because DMS reads PostgreSQL changes from the write-ahead log; the source must have wal_level set to logical and the DMS user must have replication privileges, or the CDC phase fails to start. A is wrong because a full load only task reruns the whole copy each time and never streams incremental changes. D is wrong because a Glue JDBC job is a batch extract that requires the engineer to build change detection, which is the custom work the requirement excludes. E is wrong because Amazon AppFlow connects to SaaS applications and does not support a self-managed PostgreSQL database as a source.

stem: A company must ingest opportunity records from Salesforce into an Amazon S3 data lake every hour. The data engineering team has no capacity to build or maintain connector code, and the team must filter records and mask one field during the transfer. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Create an Amazon AppFlow flow that uses Salesforce as the source, applies the filter and mask transformations, and runs hourly.
Deploy an AWS Glue Spark job that calls the Salesforce REST API, applies the transformations, and writes to Amazon S3 every hour.
Configure an AWS DMS task that uses Salesforce as the source endpoint and Amazon S3 as the target endpoint.
Use an AWS Lambda function on an hourly EventBridge schedule to page through the Salesforce API and write JSON files.

explanation: A is correct. Amazon AppFlow provides a managed Salesforce connector, a built-in hourly schedule, and record-level filter and mask transformations, so no connector code is written or maintained. B is wrong because a Glue Spark job requires the team to write and maintain Salesforce API paging, authentication, and retry logic. C is wrong because AWS DMS source endpoints are relational and NoSQL databases and streaming stores, not SaaS applications such as Salesforce. D is wrong because a Lambda function still requires custom paging, OAuth token refresh, and transformation code that the team must maintain.

stem: A data engineer must start an AWS Glue job at 02:00 local time for teams in three different time zones and must also run one-time backfill invocations on specific dates. The engineer wants a managed scheduler that handles daylight saving time and does not require an always-on server. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that uses a cron expression in UTC for each team, and manually update each rule twice a year for daylight saving time.
Run cron on an Amazon EC2 instance that calls the StartJobRun API operation for each team and for each backfill date.
Add a schedule trigger to the AWS Glue job for each team, and start the backfills by editing the trigger schedule each time.
Create an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule for each team by using a cron expression and a time zone, and one-time at() schedules for backfills.

explanation: D is correct. EventBridge Scheduler supports cron expressions with an explicit time zone and automatic daylight saving time adjustment, one-time at() schedules for backfills, and a Glue StartJobRun target, with no server to run. A is wrong because EventBridge rules evaluate cron only in UTC, so the engineer must edit each rule when daylight saving time shifts. B is wrong because an EC2 instance must be patched, monitored, and kept running, which is the operational overhead the engineer wants to avoid. C is wrong because Glue schedule triggers are cron-based in UTC and have no one-time schedule type, so backfills mean repeatedly editing production triggers.

stem: A data engineer uses an AWS Lambda function as a consumer of an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream that has 10 shards. The IteratorAge metric keeps rising, although the function's duration and error rate are normal and the shard count matches the producer volume. The engineer must increase consumer throughput without changing the shard count. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Increase the batch size of the event source mapping to 10,000 records.
Increase the memory that is allocated to the Lambda function to 10,240 MB.
Increase the parallelization factor of the event source mapping to 10.
Increase the reserved concurrency of the Lambda function to 100.

explanation: C is correct. By default Lambda runs one concurrent invocation per shard; the parallelization factor allows up to 10 concurrent batches per shard while still preserving order within each partition key, which is the only way to add consumer throughput without adding shards. A is wrong because a larger batch gives each invocation more work but still leaves one invocation per shard, so the per-shard processing rate does not improve. B is wrong because the function is not slow; duration is already normal, so more memory does not raise the number of concurrent batches per shard. D is wrong because reserved concurrency only sets a ceiling on concurrency; the poller still starts one invocation per shard, so the ceiling is never the limiting factor.

stem: An AWS Lambda function processes records from an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream. One malformed record makes the function fail, and the event source mapping retries the same batch until the records expire, which stalls the shard. The data engineer must let the good records continue to be processed and must capture the failing records for inspection. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Increase the batch size of the event source mapping so that a smaller number of batches contain the malformed record.
Configure an on-failure destination on the event source mapping that points to an Amazon SQS queue.
Turn on enhanced fan-out for the Lambda consumer of the stream.
Turn on BisectBatchOnFunctionError, and set a maximum record age and a maximum retry count.
Increase the stream's data retention period from 24 hours to 168 hours.

explanation: B is correct because an on-failure destination sends metadata about batches that exhaust their retries to an SQS queue, which gives the engineer the failing records to inspect. D is correct because bisecting the batch on error isolates the poison record into a smaller batch, and a maximum record age and retry count stop the endless retry loop so the shard advances. A is wrong because a larger batch makes the blast radius of a single bad record bigger, not smaller, and the batch still retries forever. C is wrong because enhanced fan-out changes how read throughput is allocated and has no effect on retry behavior or error handling. E is wrong because longer retention keeps the poison record available for longer and does nothing to unblock the shard.

stem: A data pipeline writes sensor readings to an Amazon DynamoDB table. Traffic is unpredictable and spikes to 20 times the average for a few minutes each day. The pipeline receives ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors during the spikes, and the team does not want to forecast capacity or pay for idle capacity. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode.
Add a global secondary index that uses the reading timestamp as the partition key.
Turn on DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table.
Increase the provisioned write capacity units to the observed peak value.

explanation: A is correct. On-demand capacity mode charges per request and absorbs sudden traffic spikes without capacity planning, which removes both the throttling and the forecasting work. B is wrong because a timestamp partition key creates a hot partition and adds write cost, since every table write is replicated to the index. C is wrong because DAX is a read-through cache and does not accelerate or absorb writes, which is where the throttling occurs. D is wrong because provisioning for the peak means paying for 20 times the needed capacity nearly all day, which the team explicitly wants to avoid.

stem: A company writes order events to an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream that has 16 shards. Producers use the store ID as the partition key, and one flagship store generates 60% of all orders. Producers receive ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors even though total traffic is well below the stream's capacity. Ordering across stores is not required. Which solution will meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Increase the shard count of the stream from 16 to 64 shards.
Change the partition key to a value that combines the store ID with a random suffix.
Change producers from PutRecord calls to PutRecords batch calls.
Turn on server-side encryption, and increase the stream's data retention period.

explanation: B is correct. The throttling is caused by a hot shard: all flagship-store records hash to one shard and exceed its 1 MB/s and 1,000 records/s write limit. Adding a random suffix spreads that store's records across many shards at no extra cost. A is wrong because quadrupling shards quadruples the cost while the flagship store's records still hash to a single shard, so the hot shard remains. C is wrong because PutRecords batches multiple records into one API call but the per-shard write limits still apply to the same hot shard. D is wrong because encryption and retention settings do not affect write throughput limits and only add cost.

stem: A nightly AWS Glue job extracts 40 tables from a production Amazon RDS for MySQL instance through a JDBC connection. Application users report slow queries while the job runs. The data engineer must stop the extraction from affecting the production workload and must keep changes to the Glue job minimal. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Reduce the Glue job to two workers so that the job opens fewer connections to the database.
Turn on AWS Glue job bookmarks so that the job reads only the rows that changed since the last run.
Create a read replica of the RDS instance, and point the Glue connection at the replica endpoint.
Increase the size of the RDS instance, and run the Glue job during the application's peak hours.

explanation: C is correct. A read replica serves the extraction from a separate instance, so the scan load never touches the primary that the application uses, and the only Glue change is the connection endpoint. A is wrong because fewer workers make the job run longer against the same primary instance, so the application is affected for a longer period. B is wrong because bookmarks reduce how many rows are read but the queries still run on the production primary, so contention remains. D is wrong because a larger instance still shares CPU, memory, and I/O between both workloads, and moving the job to peak hours makes the contention worse.

stem: A company publishes inventory change events from one application. Three teams must each receive a copy of every event and must process events at their own pace, and one team must receive only the events for a single warehouse. The company wants a serverless design that decouples the publisher from the consumers. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Write the events to a single Amazon SQS queue, and have all three teams poll the same queue and ignore the messages that they do not need.
Write the events to an Amazon S3 bucket, and have each team read the new objects from the bucket on a five-minute schedule.
Write the events to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, and create a separate message group ID for each team that receives the events.
Publish the events to an Amazon SNS topic. Subscribe an Amazon SQS queue for each team, and add a subscription filter policy.

explanation: D is correct. An SNS topic fans out each event to one SQS queue per team, each queue buffers so consumers work at their own pace, and a subscription filter policy delivers only the single warehouse's events to the team that needs them. A is wrong because an SQS message is consumed by one receiver, so the three teams would compete for messages instead of each receiving a copy. B is wrong because polling S3 on a schedule adds latency, requires each team to track which objects it has read, and provides no server-side filtering. C is wrong because message group IDs control ordering and parallelism within a FIFO queue; they do not duplicate a message to multiple consumers.

stem: A streaming pipeline reads events from an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream. A consumer bug corrupted three days of output, and the team could not reprocess the source events because the stream retained only 24 hours of data. The team must be able to replay events from the past 7 days after a future bug. Which combination of actions will meet this requirement? (Choose two.)

options.text: Turn on enhanced fan-out for every consumer application so that each application has a dedicated read throughput pipe.
Configure every consumer application to start reading from the LATEST iterator position after each deployment.
Increase the stream's data retention period to 168 hours.
Enable server-side encryption on the stream by using a customer managed AWS KMS key.
Use an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream to write a raw copy of every event to Amazon S3.

explanation: C is correct because raising retention to 168 hours keeps 7 days of records in the stream, so a consumer can be restarted at an earlier sequence number or timestamp and replay them. E is correct because a durable raw copy in Amazon S3 gives the team a replay source that survives any stream retention limit and can be reprocessed in batch. A is wrong because enhanced fan-out allocates dedicated read throughput and does not extend how long records are retained. B is wrong because starting at LATEST skips everything that arrived while the consumer was down, which is the opposite of replay. D is wrong because encryption protects the records at rest and has no effect on retention or replay.

stem: An Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream writes clickstream records to Amazon S3. The delivery stream uses a 1 MiB buffer size and a 60-second buffer interval, and it produces thousands of small objects each hour. Amazon Athena queries over the objects are slow. The company accepts up to 5 minutes of delivery delay. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Turn on dynamic partitioning on the delivery stream, and partition the output by record arrival time.
Increase the buffer size to 128 MiB and the buffer interval to 300 seconds.
Turn on Snappy compression for the delivery stream's Amazon S3 destination.
Add an AWS Lambda transform that reformats each record as JSON Lines.

explanation: B is correct. Firehose flushes when either buffering hint is reached, so raising the size to the 128 MiB maximum and the interval to 300 seconds produces far fewer, much larger objects, which is what removes the small-file overhead in Athena while staying inside the 5-minute delay budget. A is wrong because dynamic partitioning changes the S3 key layout but the same buffering hints still control object size, so the objects stay small. C is wrong because compression shrinks each object but does not reduce the number of objects that Athena must open and list. D is wrong because reformatting record content does not change how Firehose buffers or how many objects it writes.

stem: A data engineer must pull records from a partner's REST API once each hour and store them in Amazon S3. The API returns paginated results and rejects more than 10 requests per second with HTTP 429 responses. The engineer wants a serverless solution that respects the rate limit. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Run an Amazon EC2 instance with a cron job that calls the API and copies the results to Amazon S3.
Create an AWS Glue Spark job that opens one connection per executor to the API and writes the results to Amazon S3.
Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to invoke an AWS Lambda function that pages through the API with exponential backoff.
Create an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream that uses the partner API as the source and Amazon S3 as the destination.

explanation: C is correct. EventBridge Scheduler provides the managed hourly trigger, and a single Lambda function can page sequentially and apply exponential backoff on HTTP 429 responses, so there is no server to operate. A is wrong because an EC2 instance must be patched, monitored, and kept running, which is more operational overhead than a scheduled function. B is wrong because Spark executors issue requests in parallel with no coordinated rate control, which drives the request rate past the 10 requests per second limit. D is wrong because Firehose has no source type that polls an external REST API; a delivery stream receives records that are pushed to it.

stem: An AWS Glue job runs in private subnets of a VPC and must connect to a partner database that is hosted outside AWS. The partner allows connections only from a small set of static public IP addresses. The data engineer must give the Glue job a stable outbound public IP address. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Assign a public IP address to the elastic network interfaces that the Glue job creates in the private subnets.
Create a route to an internet gateway in the private subnet route table for the partner's IP address range.
Add the partner's public IP range to the inbound rules of the Glue connection's security group.
Deploy a NAT gateway that has an Elastic IP address, and route the private subnets to the NAT gateway.

explanation: D is correct. A NAT gateway with an Elastic IP address gives every outbound connection from the private subnets the same static public source address, which the partner can allowlist. A is wrong because Glue elastic network interfaces in private subnets cannot be given public IP addresses; Glue explicitly requires private subnets for VPC connections. B is wrong because a subnet with a route to an internet gateway becomes a public subnet, and instances there still need public IP addresses, which Glue interfaces do not have. C is wrong because inbound security group rules control traffic entering the VPC, while the requirement is about the source address of outbound traffic that the partner sees.

stem: A company must compute a 5-minute rolling count of failed logins per user from an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream and must emit an alert when a user exceeds a threshold. The calculation must survive application restarts without recomputing from the beginning of the stream. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use an AWS Lambda function that keeps the counts in memory and resets them on each invocation.
Use Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink with a sliding window aggregation and checkpointing turned on.
Use an AWS Glue Spark job on a 5-minute schedule that reads the whole stream on each run.
Use Amazon Data Firehose to deliver the records to Amazon S3, and query the objects with Athena every 5 minutes.

explanation: B is correct. Managed Service for Apache Flink is a managed stateful stream processor: a sliding window keeps the rolling per-user count, and checkpointing persists that state so the application resumes after a restart instead of recomputing. A is wrong because a Lambda invocation is stateless and its memory is not shared or durable, so counts are lost between invocations and across restarts. C is wrong because a Glue batch job holds no windowed state between runs and rereading the whole stream every 5 minutes is slow and expensive. D is wrong because Firehose buffering plus Athena queries adds minutes of latency and still requires the query itself to reconstruct the window from raw objects.

stem: A company runs an Amazon MSK provisioned cluster. A data engineer must deliver the records from one topic to an Amazon S3 bucket for analytics. The engineer does not want to write, deploy, or scale any consumer code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream that uses the MSK topic as the source and Amazon S3 as the destination.
Deploy a Kafka consumer application on an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group that writes objects to Amazon S3.
Create an AWS Lambda function with an Amazon MSK event source mapping that batches records into Amazon S3 objects.
Run an AWS Glue streaming job that reads from the topic and writes objects to Amazon S3.

explanation: A is correct. Amazon Data Firehose supports an Amazon MSK topic as a source and delivers buffered records to Amazon S3 with no consumer code, no scaling decisions, and no cluster to manage. B is wrong because the team must build the consumer, handle offsets and rebalancing, and operate the Auto Scaling group. C is wrong because the Lambda function code, batching logic, and failure handling are all custom code that the engineer must maintain. D is wrong because a Glue streaming job requires an ETL script and worker sizing, which is more effort than a fully managed delivery stream.

stem: A daily 60 GB compressed file lands in Amazon S3. An AWS Lambda function that aggregates the file and loads the results into Amazon Redshift now fails after 15 minutes. The data engineer must process the file reliably each day and wants a managed service that distributes the work across multiple workers. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Increase the Lambda function's memory to 10,240 MB and its ephemeral storage to 10 GB.
Split the file into 100 parts, and invoke the Lambda function one time for each part in parallel.
Replace the Lambda function with an AWS Glue Spark job that runs on a daily schedule.
Replace the Lambda function with an Amazon EC2 instance that runs the same code in a loop.

explanation: C is correct. A Glue Spark job is a managed service that has no 15-minute execution ceiling and distributes the aggregation across many workers, so the daily file completes reliably. A is wrong because the Lambda maximum execution time is 15 minutes regardless of memory or ephemeral storage, so the function still times out. B is wrong because the split is custom code the engineer must build and operate, and the aggregation across parts still has to be reassembled somewhere. D is wrong because a single EC2 instance neither distributes the work nor removes the servers the engineer must patch and monitor.

stem: A data engineer must start an AWS Step Functions state machine whenever an object with the incoming/ prefix is created in any of 12 Amazon S3 buckets. The engineer must not deploy any intermediate compute and must be able to add more buckets later. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an S3 event notification on each bucket that targets the state machine directly.
Turn on Amazon EventBridge notifications on each of the 12 buckets.
Create an Amazon SNS topic, and subscribe the state machine to the topic.
Create an EventBridge rule that matches Object Created events with the incoming/ prefix and targets the state machine.
Create an AWS Lambda function that lists the objects in each bucket every minute and starts the state machine for new objects.

explanation: B is correct because a bucket only sends events to the default event bus after EventBridge notifications are turned on for that bucket. D is correct because an EventBridge rule can filter Object Created events on the object key prefix and invoke a Step Functions state machine as a native target, so no compute sits in between. A is wrong because S3 event notification destinations are limited to Lambda, SNS, SQS, and EventBridge; a state machine is not a valid destination. C is wrong because SNS subscription protocols do not include Step Functions, so a state machine cannot subscribe to a topic. E is wrong because a polling Lambda function is exactly the intermediate compute the requirement excludes, and it adds up to a minute of latency.

stem: A company runs its transactional workload on Amazon Aurora MySQL. Analysts must query the transactional tables in Amazon Redshift within a few minutes of each change. The data engineering team does not want to build or operate an extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipeline. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a zero-ETL integration between the Aurora MySQL cluster and the Redshift data warehouse.
Create an AWS DMS task that replicates the Aurora tables to Amazon Redshift on a 5-minute schedule.
Schedule an AWS Glue job every 5 minutes that reads Aurora through JDBC and writes to Amazon Redshift.
Export Aurora snapshots to Amazon S3 every hour, and load the exported files with the COPY command.

explanation: A is correct. An Aurora MySQL zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift continuously replicates committed changes into Redshift within seconds and is fully managed, so there is no pipeline to build or run. B is wrong because a DMS task still requires the engineer to configure endpoints, monitor replication tasks, and handle failures, which is pipeline operations. C is wrong because a Glue job on a schedule is a hand-built ETL pipeline and repeated full or incremental JDBC reads add load to the transactional cluster. D is wrong because hourly snapshot exports cannot meet a few-minutes freshness requirement and add a load step to operate.

stem: A data engineer must load 5,000 gzip-compressed CSV files from an Amazon S3 prefix into an Amazon Redshift table each night. The current process issues one COPY command per file, and the load takes 6 hours. The engineer must reduce the load time without resizing the cluster. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Run all of the COPY commands inside a single transaction so that Amazon Redshift commits the work only one time.
Decompress the files before the load so that Amazon Redshift does not spend time on decompression.
Replace the COPY commands with multi-row INSERT statements that insert 1,000 rows at a time.
Run a single COPY command that points at the prefix so that Redshift loads the files in parallel.

explanation: D is correct. One COPY command against a prefix lets Amazon Redshift distribute the input files across all slices and load them in parallel, which is the documented way to load many files quickly. A is wrong because the commands still run serially; wrapping them in one transaction removes commit overhead but leaves each file loading one at a time. B is wrong because decompressing increases the bytes transferred from Amazon S3 and Redshift can read gzip files directly, so the load gets slower, not faster. C is wrong because INSERT statements bypass the parallel bulk load path and are far slower than COPY for large volumes.

stem: A company streams JSON records through an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream to Amazon S3. Analysts use Amazon Athena, and scan costs are high because every query reads whole JSON objects. The company must store the incoming records in Apache Parquet format without adding a separate transformation job. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an AWS Glue Data Catalog table that defines the schema of the records.
Add an AWS Lambda transform function to the delivery stream that rewrites each record in Apache Parquet format.
Turn on record format conversion on the delivery stream, and select Parquet as the output format.
Turn on GZIP compression for the delivery stream's Amazon S3 destination.
Run an AWS Glue crawler on the delivered objects every hour to update the table schema.

explanation: A is correct because Firehose record format conversion reads the target schema from an AWS Glue Data Catalog table, so the table must exist before conversion can be turned on. C is correct because record format conversion deserializes each JSON record and writes columnar Parquet objects natively in the delivery stream, with no separate job. B is wrong because a Lambda transform operates on individual records that Firehose then buffers, so it cannot produce a valid columnar Parquet file with a footer and row groups. D is wrong because GZIP compresses the JSON objects but leaves them row oriented, so Athena still reads every field of every record. E is wrong because a crawler catalogs objects after delivery and does not change the format that Firehose writes.

stem: A data engineer must transform small JSON files, each under 5 MB, as they arrive in Amazon S3. Roughly 200 files arrive each hour, and each transformation takes about 20 seconds of single-threaded Python code. The company wants to pay only for the time that the code runs. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Run a long-running Amazon EMR cluster with a Spark streaming application.
Run an AWS Glue Spark job with 10 G.1X workers on an hourly schedule.
Run an AWS Lambda function that processes each file as it arrives.
Poll the bucket with an Amazon ECS task on EC2.

explanation: C is correct. The work is small, short, and single threaded, so Lambda's per-millisecond billing means the company pays only for about 200 invocations of 20 seconds each hour and nothing while idle. A is wrong because a long-running EMR cluster bills for every instance hour whether or not files arrive, which is far more than the actual compute time. B is wrong because a Glue Spark job has a 1-minute minimum billing per run and provisions 10 workers that a 5 MB single-threaded task cannot use. D is wrong because the EC2 instances behind the ECS cluster run and bill continuously, and the polling loop adds cost even when no files arrive.

stem: A company runs nightly Apache Spark jobs on a long-running Amazon EMR cluster that stays provisioned at peak size all day. The jobs tolerate losing compute capacity and restarting tasks, but the cluster must not fail if capacity is reclaimed. The company must reduce the cost of the cluster. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run the primary node and the core nodes on Spot Instances.
Attach larger Amazon EBS volumes to every node in the cluster.
Store all intermediate shuffle data in HDFS on the core nodes instead of storing it in Amazon S3.
Run the task nodes on Spot Instances, and keep the primary and core nodes On-Demand.
Turn on Amazon EMR managed scaling so that the cluster adds and removes nodes with demand.

explanation: D is correct because task nodes hold no HDFS data, so losing them to a Spot interruption only causes task retries, while keeping the primary and core nodes On-Demand prevents a cluster failure. E is correct because managed scaling shrinks the cluster when the nightly jobs are not running, which removes the cost of holding peak capacity all day. A is wrong because a Spot interruption of the primary node terminates the cluster and losing core nodes loses HDFS blocks, which violates the requirement that the cluster must not fail. B is wrong because larger EBS volumes raise storage cost and do nothing about idle compute. C is wrong because shuffle data is already local to the nodes and moving storage choices does not reduce the instance hours that dominate the bill.

stem: An AWS Glue Spark job is provisioned with 50 G.2X workers so that it can handle the largest daily input. Most days the input is one tenth of that size, and Amazon CloudWatch shows that most workers are idle. The team must reduce cost without changing the job code. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Turn on AWS Glue Auto Scaling for the job, and set the maximum number of workers to 50.
Reduce the number of workers to 5, and rely on Spark to spill the data to local disk.
Change the worker type from G.2X to G.1X, and keep the job at 50 workers.
Convert the job to an AWS Glue Python shell job so that it runs on 1 DPU.

explanation: A is correct. Glue Auto Scaling adds and removes executors during the run based on the actual stage parallelism, and Glue bills only for the DPU hours the job consumes, so light days cost far less while the maximum of 50 still covers the peak day. B is wrong because five workers cannot hold the peak-day data set, and heavy spilling makes that run much longer, which raises DPU hours and risks failure. C is wrong because two G.1X workers are needed to match one G.2X worker, so 50 G.1X workers cut capacity in half rather than cutting cost on light days. D is wrong because a Python shell job has no Spark cluster and cannot run the existing distributed job code, so it violates the no-code-change constraint.

stem: An AWS Glue job in private subnets must read from an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database and write results to Amazon S3. The engineer created an AWS Glue connection, but the job times out when it starts, and the write to Amazon S3 also fails. The VPC has no NAT gateway. Which combination of actions will resolve the failures? (Choose two.)

options.text: Attach an internet gateway to the VPC, and assign a public IP address to the elastic network interfaces that the job uses.
Grant the Glue job role the AmazonS3FullAccess and AmazonRDSFullAccess managed policies.
Add a self-referencing inbound rule to the security group that the Glue connection uses.
Change the Glue connection type from JDBC to network, and remove the subnet setting.
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, and add it to the subnets' route tables.

explanation: C is correct because Glue places its elastic network interfaces in the connection's subnet and the workers must talk to one another, so the security group needs a self-referencing inbound rule for all TCP ports or the job hangs and times out at startup. E is correct because a private subnet with no NAT gateway has no route to the Amazon S3 public endpoint, and a gateway VPC endpoint adds the route table prefix list entry that makes the write succeed. A is wrong because Glue requires private subnets and does not assign public IP addresses to its network interfaces. B is wrong because the failures are network reachability problems, and broad IAM policies do not create routes or open security group rules. D is wrong because a network connection type still requires a subnet and a security group, and removing the subnet leaves Glue with nowhere to attach its interfaces.

stem: An analyst must join a small reference table that lives in Amazon RDS for MySQL with a large fact table in Amazon S3. The join runs only a few times each month. The data engineer must avoid copying the RDS table into the data lake and must avoid building a scheduled pipeline. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an AWS DMS task that replicates the RDS table into Amazon S3, and query both tables with Athena.
Create an AWS Glue job that reads the RDS table through JDBC and writes it to Amazon S3 each month.
Use Amazon Athena federated query with the MySQL data source connector to join the two tables.
Load both of the tables into Amazon Redshift, and run the join in the data warehouse each month.

explanation: C is correct. An Athena federated query uses a Lambda-based MySQL connector to read the reference table in place at query time and joins it with the S3 fact table in one SQL statement, so no copy and no pipeline exist. A is wrong because a DMS task copies the table into the data lake, which the requirement forbids, and the task must be monitored. B is wrong because a monthly Glue job is exactly the scheduled pipeline and the copy that the requirement excludes. D is wrong because loading both tables into Redshift copies the data and adds a warehouse to operate for a query that runs a few times a month.

stem: An AWS Glue Spark job fails during a large join with a No space left on device error. Amazon CloudWatch metrics show that the job exhausts local disk during the shuffle stage, although memory use stays normal. The engineer must make the job complete without adding workers. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Turn on the Amazon S3 shuffle plugin so that Glue writes the shuffle data to Amazon S3.
Increase the job's timeout so that the shuffle stage has more time to finish.
Turn on AWS Glue job bookmarks so that the job reads fewer input files.
Set the job's worker type to Standard so that each worker runs more executors.

explanation: A is correct. The Glue cloud shuffle storage plugin writes shuffle spill to Amazon S3 instead of the worker's local disk, which removes the local disk ceiling that is causing the failure without changing the worker count. B is wrong because the job is failing on disk capacity, not on elapsed time, so a longer timeout changes nothing. C is wrong because bookmarks skip already-processed input, which does not apply here and does not change how much intermediate shuffle data the join produces for the current data. D is wrong because a Standard worker packs two executors onto the same 1 DPU and 50 GB of local disk, so each executor gets less disk than on G.1X and the spill gets worse.

stem: A company already runs an Amazon EKS cluster for its microservices and has spare capacity on the cluster. A data engineering team must run Apache Spark jobs and wants to use the same cluster instead of provisioning separate compute. The team also wants AWS to manage the Spark runtime and job submission. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Install and maintain an open source Spark operator on the Amazon EKS cluster, and build and patch custom Spark container images.
Run Spark on Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type, and share the EKS node group.
Create an Amazon EMR cluster on Amazon EC2 in the same subnets as the EKS cluster.
Use Amazon EMR on EKS to submit the Spark jobs to a virtual cluster on the EKS cluster.

explanation: D is correct. EMR on EKS registers a virtual cluster against a namespace in the existing EKS cluster and runs jobs with the AWS-managed EMR Spark runtime and the StartJobRun API, so the team reuses the spare capacity without operating Spark itself. A is wrong because the team then owns the operator, the images, and the Spark version upgrades, which is the management the requirement gives to AWS. B is wrong because ECS and EKS are separate orchestrators; an ECS task cannot run on an EKS node group. C is wrong because an EMR cluster on EC2 provisions separate compute rather than using the spare EKS capacity.

stem: A data engineer runs containerized batch transformation tasks on Amazon ECS. The tasks are idempotent, can be restarted at any time, and run for about 10 minutes each. The team does not want to manage EC2 instances and must reduce compute cost. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Run the tasks on the Amazon EC2 launch type with On-Demand Instances.
Run the tasks on AWS Fargate Spot capacity, and retry any task that is interrupted.
Run the tasks on AWS Fargate with the default On-Demand capacity provider.
Run the tasks on the Amazon EC2 launch type with Reserved Instances for steady capacity.

explanation: B is correct. Fargate Spot offers the deepest discount on Fargate capacity and suits idempotent, restartable, short tasks, and it keeps the serverless model so no EC2 instances are managed. A is wrong because On-Demand EC2 capacity is more expensive than Fargate Spot and still requires the team to manage the instances and the capacity provider. C is wrong because Fargate On-Demand meets the no-instance-management requirement but costs substantially more than Fargate Spot for interruption-tolerant work. D is wrong because Reserved Instances commit to steady capacity for a bursty batch workload and still leave EC2 instances to manage.

stem: A company stores millions of free-text customer reviews in Amazon S3. A data engineer must add a sentiment label and a two-sentence summary to each review as part of a nightly pipeline. The team has no machine learning engineers and does not want to train or host a model. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Train a text classification model in Amazon SageMaker AI, and host the model behind a real-time endpoint.
Deploy an open source large language model on Amazon EC2 GPU instances, and call the model from the pipeline.
Call an Amazon Bedrock foundation model from the pipeline with a prompt that returns the label and the summary.
Use Amazon Kendra to index the reviews, and query the index for the label and summary of each review.

explanation: C is correct. Amazon Bedrock exposes managed foundation models through an API, so a single prompt produces both the sentiment label and the summary with no training, no endpoint, and no infrastructure. A is wrong because training and hosting a SageMaker model requires labeled data and machine learning skills the team does not have, and a real-time endpoint runs continuously. B is wrong because self-hosting a model on GPU instances means the team owns capacity planning, scaling, and patching. D is wrong because Amazon Kendra is an intelligent search service that retrieves relevant documents; it does not generate a summary or a sentiment label for every record.

stem: A nightly AWS Glue job calls an Amazon Bedrock model to enrich 40 million records. The job hits throttling limits and does not finish before the morning reporting window. The results are not needed until the following day, and the team wants the lowest possible inference cost. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Submit the records to Amazon Bedrock as a batch inference job that writes the results to Amazon S3.
Purchase provisioned throughput for the model, and keep the per-record calls in the Glue job.
Increase the number of AWS Glue workers so that the job issues more concurrent inference requests.
Add exponential backoff to the Glue job, and retry each throttled request up to 10 times.

explanation: A is correct. Amazon Bedrock batch inference processes a large set of records asynchronously from Amazon S3 at a discount to on-demand pricing, which fits a workload whose results are needed only the next day and removes the per-request throttling problem. B is wrong because provisioned throughput reserves capacity at an hourly commitment that costs far more than batch inference for a job that runs once a night. C is wrong because more workers push more concurrent requests at the same account quota, so throttling gets worse rather than better. D is wrong because backoff and retries only slow the job down; the aggregate request rate still exceeds the quota and inference cost is unchanged.

stem: A company keeps 200,000 internal policy documents in Amazon S3. A data engineer must build an application that answers employee questions in natural language and cites the source documents. The team wants a managed retrieval augmented generation workflow and does not want to write chunking or retrieval code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Fine-tune an Amazon Bedrock foundation model on the documents, and query the fine-tuned model.
Load the documents into Amazon Redshift, and let the application generate SQL queries against the tables.
Use an AWS Glue job to chunk documents, generate embeddings, and index them in Amazon OpenSearch Service.
Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that uses the S3 bucket as a data source, and query the knowledge base.

explanation: D is correct. An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base ingests an S3 data source, handles chunking, embedding, and vector storage automatically, and returns generated answers with citations to the source documents. A is wrong because fine-tuning changes model behavior rather than grounding answers in specific documents, and it cannot cite sources or reflect newly added documents. B is wrong because policy documents are unstructured text and a SQL warehouse offers no semantic retrieval over them. C is wrong because it works but requires the team to build and maintain the chunking, embedding, indexing, and retrieval code that the requirement excludes.

stem: An AWS Lambda function must run SQL statements in an Amazon Redshift Serverless workgroup and return the results to a web application. The developer wants to avoid managing database connections, JDBC drivers, and long-lived credentials inside the function. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Package a JDBC driver in the deployment package, and read the password from AWS Secrets Manager.
Call the Amazon Redshift Data API from the function, and authorize the calls with the function's IAM role.
Place the function in the workgroup's VPC, and open a persistent ODBC connection at cold start.
Run the SQL statements from an Amazon EC2 instance, and have the function call the instance.

explanation: B is correct. The Redshift Data API is an HTTPS API that requires no driver, no persistent connection, and no VPC attachment, and it authorizes requests with IAM, so the function needs no stored database password. A is wrong because the function still opens and manages JDBC connections and still handles a password, which is the work the developer wants to avoid. C is wrong because a persistent ODBC connection from a Lambda execution environment is fragile, requires VPC networking, and leaves connection management in the function. D is wrong because an EC2 instance adds a server to patch and scale and does not remove the driver or credential handling.

stem: A data engineer must expose a curated dataset in an Amazon DynamoDB table as a read-only REST API for partner systems. Traffic is low but unpredictable. The engineer wants to avoid writing and maintaining any compute code for the API. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS service integration that calls the DynamoDB Query operation.
Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API that invokes an AWS Lambda function that queries the table and formats the response.
Run a container on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer that queries the table.
Turn on DynamoDB Streams, and let the partners read the stream records directly from the table.

explanation: A is correct. An API Gateway AWS service integration calls DynamoDB directly with a mapping template and an IAM role, so there is no function code to write, test, or patch. B is wrong because the Lambda function is compute code the engineer must maintain, which the requirement excludes. C is wrong because a container image, a task definition, and a load balancer are all additional components to build and operate for a low-traffic API. D is wrong because DynamoDB Streams provides a time-ordered feed of item changes for internal consumers, not a queryable REST interface for partners.

stem: Producers write Avro records to an Amazon MSK topic, and consumers fail whenever a producer adds a field. The data engineer must validate that each new producer schema stays backward compatible before records reach the topic, and must let consumers resolve the schema for each record. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Store the schema in an Amazon S3 object that each consumer reads at startup.
Run an AWS Glue crawler on the topic every hour to detect schema changes in the records.
Register the schema in the AWS Glue Schema Registry, and set the compatibility mode to backward.
Convert the records to JSON so that consumers can ignore the fields that they do not recognize.

explanation: C is correct. The AWS Glue Schema Registry validates a new schema version against the configured backward compatibility rule at serialization time and rejects breaking changes, and its serializer embeds a schema version ID that consumers use to resolve the writer schema. A is wrong because an S3 object provides no compatibility enforcement and a consumer that reads only at startup misses later versions. B is wrong because Glue crawlers catalog data stores such as Amazon S3 and JDBC sources; they do not crawl Kafka topics or block incompatible producers. D is wrong because changing the wire format loses Avro's typed schema evolution and still allows a producer to publish a breaking change.

stem: A data engineer designs a landing zone for streaming records. Downstream jobs always read complete records rather than a few columns, the record schema changes often, and records must be appended continuously with fast writes. The engineer must choose an open file format for the landing zone. Which format will meet these requirements?

options.text: Apache Parquet
Apache ORC
Gzip-compressed CSV
Apache Avro

explanation: D is correct. Avro is a row-based, splittable binary format that stores the writer schema with the data and supports schema evolution, so it fits append-heavy writes, frequent schema changes, and whole-record reads. A is wrong because Parquet is columnar and optimized for reading a subset of columns; writing it requires buffering row groups, which slows continuous appends. B is wrong because ORC is also columnar and carries the same buffering cost, so it gives no benefit when every column is read anyway. C is wrong because a gzip-compressed CSV object is not splittable, carries no typed schema, and cannot express schema evolution.

stem: A company already loads raw sales data into Amazon Redshift.
