A nightly process exports the raw tables to Amazon S3, runs an AWS Glue Spark job that aggregates the data, and loads the results back into Redshift. The company must simplify the process and reduce data movement. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Replace the AWS Glue job with a transient Amazon EMR cluster that reads from Amazon Redshift through the Spark connector.
Replace the AWS Glue job with an AWS Lambda function that reads the exported files from Amazon S3.
Keep the AWS Glue job, and use Redshift Spectrum to query the exported files in Amazon S3.
Replace the export and the Glue job with an Amazon Redshift stored procedure that a scheduled query runs.

explanation: D is correct. The aggregation is relational work on data that already sits in Redshift, so a stored procedure driven by a Redshift scheduled query removes the export, the Spark job, and the reload entirely. A is wrong because an EMR cluster still pulls the data out of Redshift and adds a cluster to size and operate. B is wrong because it keeps the export step, and a single Lambda function cannot aggregate a large warehouse table within its 15-minute limit. C is wrong because it keeps both the export and the Glue job and simply adds an external query path, so data movement is unchanged.

stem: An AWS Glue Spark job reads a Data Catalog table that is partitioned by year, month, and day and holds five years of data. The job needs only the most recent day, but it currently reads every partition and runs for hours. The engineer must reduce the amount of data that the job reads. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Add a Spark filter on the date column after the job creates the DynamicFrame from the catalog.
Pass a push-down predicate on the partition columns when the job creates the DynamicFrame.
Increase the number of workers so that Spark reads the partitions in parallel.
Run an AWS Glue crawler before the job so that the catalog contains fresh partitions.

explanation: B is correct. A push-down predicate is evaluated against the Data Catalog partition metadata before any objects are listed or opened, so Glue reads only the objects under the requested day's partition. A is wrong because the filter runs after the DynamicFrame is created, so all five years of objects are still read from Amazon S3 before any rows are discarded. C is wrong because more workers spread the same full scan across more executors, which raises DPU cost without reducing bytes read. D is wrong because a crawler registers partitions in the catalog and does not influence which partitions the job chooses to read.

stem: A company merges customer records from three acquired systems into one Amazon S3 dataset. The systems have no shared customer key, and names and addresses are entered inconsistently, so exact-match joins leave duplicates. The data engineer must identify the records that refer to the same customer. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Create an AWS Glue job that joins the datasets on a hash of the customer name and the postal code.
Load the datasets into Amazon Redshift, and run a SELECT DISTINCT statement over all of the columns.
Use the AWS Glue FindMatches ML transform to label and match records across the datasets.
Use an AWS Glue crawler to classify the datasets, and rely on the crawler to merge the schemas.

explanation: C is correct. FindMatches is a Glue machine learning transform for record linkage: an engineer labels a sample of matching and non-matching pairs, and the transform then finds fuzzy duplicates across datasets that share no key. A is wrong because a hash is an exact-match technique, so any spelling or formatting difference produces a different hash and the duplicate is missed. B is wrong because SELECT DISTINCT removes only byte-identical rows and cannot recognize inconsistent spellings of the same customer. D is wrong because a crawler infers schemas and partitions; it does not compare or deduplicate record values.

stem: A data engineering team runs several AWS Glue Spark jobs that read thousands of uncompressed CSV objects from Amazon S3 and write uncompressed CSV output. Job runtimes and Amazon Athena scan costs are both rising. The team must reduce processing cost and query cost without buying more workers. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Convert the datasets to Apache Parquet with Snappy compression.
Store the output in the Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class.
Partition the output by the column that queries filter on most often.
Increase the number of G.2X workers on every job to shorten the total runtime.
Turn on versioning on the output bucket so that reprocessing does not duplicate data.

explanation: A is correct because columnar Parquet with Snappy compression cuts the bytes that Spark reads and that Athena scans, which lowers both DPU hours and per-query scan charges. C is correct because partitioning on the common filter column lets Glue and Athena prune whole prefixes so neither engine reads data the query does not need. B is wrong because Glacier Flexible Retrieval objects are not directly queryable by Athena and require a restore before use. D is wrong because more workers roughly hold DPU hours constant while raising the per-run rate, so cost does not fall and Athena scans are unchanged. E is wrong because versioning keeps previous object versions and increases storage cost without affecting processing or query cost.

stem: A company runs 60 Apache Airflow DAGs on self-managed servers in its data center. The company must move the orchestration to AWS, must keep the existing DAG code unchanged, and must stop patching Airflow servers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Rewrite each DAG as an AWS Step Functions state machine, and start the state machines with EventBridge rules.
Upload the DAGs to an Amazon S3 bucket, and run them in an Amazon MWAA environment.
Install Airflow on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer.
Convert each DAG to an AWS Glue workflow that chains the equivalent jobs and triggers.

explanation: B is correct. Amazon MWAA runs managed Apache Airflow, picks up DAG files from an S3 bucket, and handles the scheduler, workers, and patching, so the 60 DAGs run unchanged. A is wrong because rewriting 60 DAGs in Amazon States Language is a large migration effort and discards the existing code. C is wrong because the company still owns Airflow installation, upgrades, and OS patching on the EC2 instances. D is wrong because Glue workflows use a different trigger and job model, so every DAG must be rebuilt, and Glue workflows cannot express arbitrary Python operators.

stem: A data engineer builds a serverless workflow that runs an AWS Glue job, waits for the job to finish, and then loads the results into Amazon Redshift. A single run takes about 2 hours, and the team runs the workflow 30 times each day. The team needs a full execution history for auditing. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use an AWS Step Functions Standard Workflow with the AWS Glue service integration.
Use an AWS Step Functions Express Workflow, and send the logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
Use an AWS Lambda function that polls the Glue job status in a loop until the job finishes.
Use an Amazon EventBridge rule that starts each step at a fixed time offset from the previous step.

explanation: A is correct. A Standard Workflow runs for up to a year, records a durable execution history that satisfies the audit requirement, and its Glue service integration waits for the job to finish without custom polling. B is wrong because an Express Workflow is limited to 5 minutes of run time and does not keep an execution history in Step Functions, so a 2-hour run fails. C is wrong because a Lambda function cannot poll for 2 hours within its 15-minute limit and provides no built-in execution history. D is wrong because fixed time offsets are guesses; a slow Glue job would make the load step start before the data is ready.

stem: An AWS Step Functions state machine calls a third-party API that intermittently returns HTTP 503 errors. The workflow fails whenever the API returns an error, and an engineer restarts the workflow by hand. The workflow must recover from transient errors on its own and must send permanent failures to a cleanup state. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add a Retry field to the task with an exponential backoff rate and a maximum attempt count.
Add a Wait state of 300 seconds before the task so that the API has time to recover.
Change the state machine from a Standard Workflow to an Express Workflow.
Add a Catch field to the task that routes the error to the cleanup state.
Send the failed executions to an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue for automatic retry.

explanation: A is correct because a Retry field with a backoff rate makes the task retry transient HTTP 503 errors automatically and space the attempts out, which removes the manual restart. D is correct because a Catch field transfers the execution to the cleanup state after the retries are exhausted, so permanent failures are handled inside the workflow. B is wrong because a fixed wait before every call slows all executions and does nothing when the API fails during the call. C is wrong because the workflow type controls duration and history semantics, not error handling. E is wrong because Step Functions has no dead-letter queue for whole executions, and an SQS queue cannot resume a failed execution.

stem: A data engineer must notify an on-call email distribution list within one minute whenever any AWS Glue job in an account changes to the FAILED state. The engineer must not modify the Glue job scripts. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Add a try-except block to every AWS Glue job script that publishes a message to an Amazon SNS topic when the job fails.
Schedule an AWS Lambda function every minute to call GetJobRuns and send email through Amazon SES.
Create an EventBridge rule that matches Glue Job State Change events with a FAILED state and targets an SNS topic.
Create an Amazon CloudWatch Logs subscription filter on the Glue log group that writes to an Amazon SQS queue.

explanation: C is correct. AWS Glue emits a Glue Job State Change event to the default EventBridge event bus, and a rule that filters on the FAILED state and targets an SNS topic delivers email within seconds with no code and no script changes. A is wrong because editing every job script is the change the requirement forbids, and a job that fails on out-of-memory never reaches the except block. B is wrong because a polling function is custom code to maintain and adds up to a minute of avoidable delay. D is wrong because a subscription filter delivers matching log lines to a queue, which no one reads as email, and it requires the failure to be visible in the log text.

stem: A data engineer must start an AWS Step Functions workflow for each Amazon DynamoDB Streams record whose eventName value is MODIFY. The engineer wants to avoid writing and maintaining any glue code between the stream and the workflow. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function with a DynamoDB Streams event source mapping that filters the records and starts the workflow.
Create an EventBridge pipe that uses the stream as the source, filters on eventName, and targets the workflow.
Create an EventBridge rule that matches DynamoDB Streams records and targets the workflow.
Turn on Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB, and poll the stream from inside the workflow.

explanation: B is correct. An EventBridge pipe reads a DynamoDB stream as a source, applies a content filter on eventName, and invokes a Step Functions state machine as the target, so the point-to-point integration needs no code. A is wrong because the Lambda function is exactly the glue code the requirement excludes, even though event source mapping filters can narrow the records. C is wrong because DynamoDB Streams records are not published to an EventBridge event bus, so a rule never matches them. D is wrong because Step Functions has no stream poller, and a workflow cannot subscribe to a Kinesis stream.

stem: An ingestion API invokes an AWS Lambda function that loads records into Amazon RDS. During traffic spikes the function throttles and records are lost, and the team cannot inspect the records that failed. The team must absorb the spikes and must retain the records that the function cannot process. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Put an Amazon SQS queue between the API and the function as the function's event source.
Increase the Lambda function's timeout to 15 minutes.
Increase the size of the RDS instance, and add a read replica to handle the additional traffic.
Turn on AWS X-Ray tracing for the Lambda function.
Configure a dead-letter queue on the source queue with a maximum receive count.

explanation: A is correct because an SQS queue buffers the spike and lets Lambda drain messages at its own concurrency, so nothing is dropped when the function cannot keep up. E is correct because a redrive policy with a maximum receive count moves messages that repeatedly fail into a dead-letter queue, which preserves them for inspection. B is wrong because a longer timeout does not add concurrency and does not store records that were never accepted. C is wrong because the loss happens at the Lambda invocation layer, and a read replica does not serve writes. D is wrong because X-Ray provides traces for diagnosis but does not buffer or retain any record.

stem: An AWS Lambda function that an Amazon SQS standard queue invokes loads records into Amazon Redshift. Because a standard queue can deliver the same message more than one time, some records are loaded twice. The engineer must prevent duplicate loads without changing the queue type. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Record each processed message ID in an Amazon DynamoDB table, and skip the IDs that already exist.
Increase the queue's visibility timeout to six times the function's timeout.
Set the function's reserved concurrency to 1 so that only one batch is processed at a time.
Turn on long polling on the queue so that the consumer receives each message only one time.

explanation: A is correct. A conditional write of the message ID to a DynamoDB table makes the load idempotent, so a redelivered message is recognized and skipped regardless of why the duplicate occurred. B is wrong because a longer visibility timeout reduces duplicates caused by slow processing but does not eliminate the at-least-once delivery that standard queues guarantee. C is wrong because serializing the consumer lowers throughput and a redelivered message is still processed a second time. D is wrong because long polling controls how the ReceiveMessage call waits for messages; it does not provide exactly-once delivery.

stem: A pipeline must send a failure notification to an on-call email address and at the same time start an AWS Lambda function that opens a ticket in an external system. The team must be able to add more notification targets later without changing the pipeline code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Send the notification to an Amazon SQS queue, and have the email client and the Lambda function poll the queue for messages.
Write the notification to an Amazon S3 object, and configure event notifications for the email address.
Send the notification with Amazon SES, and have the Lambda function parse the outgoing message.
Publish the notification to an Amazon SNS topic, and subscribe the email address and the function to the topic.

explanation: D is correct. SNS delivers each published message to every subscriber, so the email endpoint and the Lambda function both receive the notification, and new targets are added by creating subscriptions rather than by editing the pipeline. A is wrong because an SQS message is consumed by a single receiver and an email client cannot poll an SQS queue. B is wrong because S3 event notifications cannot deliver to an arbitrary email address; SNS or SES would still be required. C is wrong because SES sends email but gives the Lambda function no delivery path, and parsing outbound mail is a fragile coupling.

stem: An AWS Step Functions workflow must process 3 million Amazon S3 objects by invoking an AWS Lambda function for each object. The team first used an inline Map state, and the workflow failed because of the concurrency limit and the size of the execution history. The engineer must process all of the objects in one workflow. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Split the object list into 100 batches, and run 100 workflow executions from a driver function.
Replace the Map state with a Parallel state that contains 40 identical branches.
Increase the Lambda function's memory and timeout so that each invocation handles more objects.
Replace the inline Map state with a distributed map state that reads the object list from Amazon S3.

explanation: D is correct. A distributed map state reads the item list directly from Amazon S3, runs up to 10,000 parallel child executions, and keeps each child's history separate, so it scales past the inline Map concurrency ceiling and the 25,000-event history limit. A is wrong because it abandons the single-workflow requirement and adds a driver function and batch bookkeeping to maintain. B is wrong because a Parallel state runs a fixed set of branches inside the same execution, so the history limit still applies and 40 branches do not scale to 3 million items. C is wrong because the concurrency and history limits are properties of the state machine, not of the function's memory or timeout.

stem: An AWS Step Functions workflow starts an AWS Glue job and must not run the next step until the Glue job finishes. The current design uses an AWS Lambda function in a loop that calls GetJobRun every 30 seconds, which adds cost and code to maintain. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Add a Wait state that pauses for the Glue job's average runtime before the next step runs.
Configure the Glue job to start the next step through an Amazon SNS notification when it ends.
Call the Glue job through the optimized service integration with the .sync request pattern.
Move the polling loop into the Glue job's own script so that the job reports its own status.

explanation: C is correct. The glue:startJobRun.sync optimized integration makes Step Functions start the job and hold the state until the job reaches a terminal status, so the polling function and its code disappear. A is wrong because a fixed wait is a guess; a slower-than-average run lets the next step read incomplete output. B is wrong because it requires adding notification code to the job and a listener to resume the workflow, which is more moving parts than a built-in integration. D is wrong because the loop still exists, it now runs inside billed Glue DPU time, and the workflow still has no way to wait.

stem: An AWS Lambda function that Amazon S3 event notifications invoke opens a connection to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. During bulk uploads, hundreds of concurrent invocations exhaust the database's connection limit and other applications fail. The engineer must cap the number of simultaneous database connections that the function can open. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Set a reserved concurrency limit on the Lambda function.
Set a provisioned concurrency value on the Lambda function.
Increase the Lambda function's timeout so that the invocations queue.
Increase the Lambda function's memory so that the invocations finish sooner.

explanation: A is correct. Reserved concurrency sets a hard ceiling on how many execution environments of the function run at once, so it directly bounds the number of database connections the function can hold. B is wrong because provisioned concurrency pre-initializes environments to remove cold starts; it does not cap total concurrency, which can still scale above the provisioned value. C is wrong because a longer timeout keeps each connection open for longer, which makes connection exhaustion worse rather than better. D is wrong because faster invocations reduce the duration of each connection but Lambda still scales out to hundreds of concurrent environments during the upload.

stem: An AWS Lambda function serves a data API and must respond in under 100 milliseconds. The function imports a large Python library during initialization, and users see occasional one-second responses when traffic rises after an idle period. The engineer must remove the initialization delay. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Increase the function's reserved concurrency to the expected peak value.
Move the library import inside the handler function.
Configure provisioned concurrency, and use Application Auto Scaling to adjust it.
Increase the function's timeout, and add retries in the client application.

explanation: C is correct. Provisioned concurrency keeps initialized execution environments warm so the import cost is paid ahead of the request, and Application Auto Scaling adjusts the provisioned count as traffic changes. A is wrong because reserved concurrency only reserves a share of the account concurrency limit; new environments still cold start. B is wrong because moving the import into the handler shifts the same work into the request path, so every invocation pays it instead of only cold ones. D is wrong because a longer timeout and client retries hide the symptom while the user-visible latency stays above the 100-millisecond target.

stem: An AWS Lambda function must read and write a shared 20 GB reference dataset across invocations, and several functions must see the same files. The team must not redesign the functions to use object storage APIs and needs POSIX file access. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Increase ephemeral storage to 10,240 MB. Copy the dataset at cold start.
Mount an Amazon EFS file system on the functions through an EFS access point.
Attach an Amazon EBS volume to each function's execution environment.
Store the dataset in Amazon S3, and mount the bucket with Mountpoint inside the function.

explanation: B is correct. Lambda can mount an Amazon EFS file system through an access point, which gives every function POSIX read and write access to the same shared files with no size limit at the 20 GB scale. A is wrong because /tmp holds at most 10,240 MB, which cannot store a 20 GB dataset, and the storage is private to one execution environment. C is wrong because Lambda execution environments do not support attaching EBS volumes. D is wrong because Mountpoint for Amazon S3 needs FUSE kernel support that the Lambda execution environment does not provide, and it would still be object storage semantics rather than POSIX.

stem: A data engineering team deploys AWS Glue jobs, Amazon S3 buckets, and IAM roles by hand in three accounts, and the environments have drifted apart. The team writes Python and wants to define the infrastructure with reusable, typed components that produce AWS CloudFormation stacks. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Write shell scripts that call the AWS CLI, and run the scripts in each of the accounts.
Write raw AWS CloudFormation templates in YAML, and copy the templates between accounts.
Define the resources with the AWS CDK in Python, and deploy the synthesized stacks.
Create an AWS Service Catalog portfolio, and let engineers launch the products manually.

explanation: C is correct. The AWS CDK lets the team write typed Python constructs that can be reused across accounts and synthesizes them into CloudFormation stacks, which removes both the manual steps and the drift. A is wrong because imperative CLI scripts have no desired-state model, so drift and partial failures are not detected or corrected. B is wrong because copied YAML templates are duplicated rather than reused, and they cannot be composed as typed Python components. D is wrong because Service Catalog governs which products users can launch but still depends on underlying templates and keeps the launch step manual.

stem: A team builds a serverless pipeline that consists of AWS Lambda functions, an Amazon EventBridge rule, and an Amazon SQS queue. The team wants short template syntax for serverless resources, one command that packages function code to Amazon S3, and local testing of the functions before deployment. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS CloudFormation templates, and upload the function code to Amazon S3 by hand.
Use AWS SAM templates with the sam build, sam local invoke, and sam deploy commands.
Use the AWS CDK. Test the functions by deploying to a sandbox account.
Use the AWS Management Console, and export the finished stack as a template.

explanation: B is correct. AWS SAM adds shorthand resource types such as AWS::Serverless::Function, sam build and sam deploy package and upload the code automatically, and sam local invoke runs the functions in a local container before deployment. A is wrong because plain CloudFormation has no serverless shorthand, no packaging command, and no local invocation support. C is wrong because the CDK has no local function invocation, so every test requires a deployment, which the requirement rules out. D is wrong because console clicks are not repeatable, and an exported template still leaves packaging and local testing unsolved.

stem: A team stores AWS Glue job scripts in a GitHub repository and copies the scripts to Amazon S3 by hand. Untested changes have broken production jobs twice. The team must run unit tests automatically on every commit and must promote only the changes that pass. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Require two manual approvers to review a checklist before anyone copies a script.
Create an AWS CodePipeline pipeline that uses the GitHub repository as its source stage.
Schedule an AWS Lambda function to copy the newest scripts to Amazon S3 every hour.
Add an AWS CodeBuild stage that runs the unit tests and fails the pipeline on any error.
Run the unit tests inside each AWS Glue job at the start of the run, and stop the job when a test fails.

explanation: B is correct because a CodePipeline source stage connected to GitHub starts the pipeline automatically on every commit, which is the trigger the requirement needs. D is correct because a CodeBuild test stage runs the unit tests and a non-zero exit code stops the pipeline, so only passing changes reach the deploy stage. A is wrong because a human checklist is not automated testing and did not prevent the two outages. C is wrong because an hourly copy promotes untested code on a timer with no quality gate at all. E is wrong because the code is already in production when those tests run, so a failure has already replaced the working script.

stem: An AWS Glue Spark job fails intermittently, and the logs appear only after the job ends, so the engineer cannot tell which stage fails. The engineer must stream driver and executor logs to Amazon CloudWatch while the job runs and must inspect Spark stage and task details after each failure. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Turn on AWS CloudTrail data events for the job's Amazon S3 prefixes.
Turn on continuous logging in the job's configuration.
Turn on AWS X-Ray tracing for the Glue job, and view the service map.
Turn on the Spark UI for the job, and write the Spark event logs to an Amazon S3 path.
Add print statements throughout the script, and read the output on the job run details page after the run ends.

explanation: B is correct because continuous logging streams driver and executor log messages to CloudWatch Logs while the run is in progress instead of flushing them at the end. D is correct because enabling the Spark UI writes Spark event logs to Amazon S3 so the engineer can open the history server and inspect stage, task, and executor detail after a failure. A is wrong because CloudTrail data events record S3 API calls, not Spark application behavior. C is wrong because AWS Glue jobs do not support X-Ray tracing of Spark stages, and a service map would not show task-level detail. E is wrong because print output is buffered into the same end-of-run logs, so it does not give live visibility or Spark stage detail.

stem: An AWS Lambda function that parses a 200 MB file is CPU-bound and takes 40 seconds at its current 512 MB memory setting. The team must reduce the runtime and is willing to test several configurations to find the best one. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Increase the function's timeout from 60 seconds to 900 seconds.
Increase the function's ephemeral storage from 512 MB to 2,048 MB.
Increase the function's memory setting so that the function receives more vCPU.
Increase the function's reserved concurrency so that more invocations run in parallel.

explanation: C is correct. Lambda allocates CPU proportionally to the configured memory, so raising the memory setting gives a CPU-bound function more vCPU and shortens the run, and the shorter duration often offsets the higher per-millisecond price. A is wrong because the timeout is only a limit on how long an invocation may run; it does not make the code execute faster. B is wrong because ephemeral storage is disk space in /tmp and has no effect on CPU allocation. D is wrong because concurrency governs how many invocations run at the same time, not how quickly one 200 MB file is parsed.

stem: A data engineer must run a 200 MB pandas transformation one time each day. The code is single-threaded Python, runs for about 25 minutes, and does not benefit from a cluster. The engineer must run the code on a managed service at the lowest cost. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Run an AWS Glue Python shell job with 1 DPU.
Run an AWS Glue Spark job with 10 G.1X workers.
Run the code on a persistent Amazon EMR cluster with one core node.
Run the code in an AWS Lambda function with 512 MB of memory.

explanation: A is correct. A Glue Python shell job runs plain Python with pandas on a single 1 DPU worker, is billed only for the minutes it runs, and has no 15-minute execution limit, so a 25-minute daily run is cheap and fully managed. B is wrong because ten Spark workers cost roughly an order of magnitude more and a single-threaded script cannot use them. C is wrong because a persistent EMR cluster bills for instance hours all day for a job that runs 25 minutes. D is wrong because the Lambda maximum execution time is 15 minutes, so a 25-minute run cannot complete.

stem: An AWS Glue Spark job writes its output with 2,000 tasks and produces 2,000 small Apache Parquet objects on each run. Amazon Athena queries over the output are slow because of the object count. The engineer must reduce the number of output objects without changing how the job reads and processes its input. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Change the job's worker type from G.1X to G.2X so that each worker has more memory and writes larger objects.
Turn on job bookmarks so that each run writes only the new records.
Write the output as gzip-compressed CSV instead of Apache Parquet.
Call coalesce or repartition on the DataFrame before the write to reduce the output partitions.

explanation: D is correct. Spark writes one object per output partition, so reducing the partition count with coalesce or repartition immediately before the write produces far fewer and larger objects without touching the read or transform logic. A is wrong because the number of written objects follows the partition count, not the worker size, so a bigger worker type still writes 2,000 objects. B is wrong because bookmarks change which input rows are read, which alters the job's processing behavior and still writes one object per partition. C is wrong because changing the format does not change the object count and gzip CSV is neither columnar nor splittable, so Athena gets slower.

stem: An AWS Lambda function enriches 100,000 incoming records for each invocation by searching a 50,000-item Python list for each record's product ID. The function times out, and profiling shows that almost all of the time is spent in the lookup loop. The engineer must reduce the runtime without adding memory or services. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Sort the list of records by product ID before the enrichment loop runs.
Move the lookup list into an environment variable of the function.
Wrap the lookup loop in a try-except block for missing IDs.
Load the lookup data into a dictionary that is keyed by product ID.

explanation: D is correct. Searching a list is a linear scan, so the work is 100,000 times 50,000 comparisons; a dictionary is a hash table with average constant-time lookup, which reduces the enrichment to roughly 100,000 operations. A is wrong because sorting the records does not change how each lookup searches the list, and a plain list scan cannot exploit the order. B is wrong because an environment variable stores the same data as a string that still must be scanned, and it is limited to 4 KB of environment size. C is wrong because exception handling changes control flow for missing keys and does nothing about the cost of the scan itself.

stem: A gaming company stores player session state in a key-value store. Reads must complete in microseconds, and writes must complete in single-digit milliseconds. Acknowledged writes must survive the failure of a node without data loss, because the session state is not persisted anywhere else. Which AWS service will meet these requirements?

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) with a replica in a second Availability Zone
Amazon MemoryDB
Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity mode
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment

explanation: B is correct. Amazon MemoryDB is a durable in-memory database that serves reads in microseconds and writes in single-digit milliseconds, and it commits every write to a Multi-AZ transaction log before acknowledging it, so acknowledged writes survive a node failure. A is wrong because ElastiCache replication is asynchronous, so writes that the primary already acknowledged can be lost when a replica is promoted. C is wrong because DynamoDB delivers single-digit millisecond read latency, not microsecond latency. D is wrong because a disk-backed relational engine cannot serve microsecond reads, and the Multi-AZ standby only provides failover rather than lower latency.

stem: A logistics company tracks 50 million packages. An API looks up a single package by tracking number and must respond in single-digit milliseconds at 40,000 requests per second. Traffic is steady. The company runs no joins and no ad hoc SQL queries on this data. Which data store will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: An Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster with several read replicas
An Amazon Redshift table that uses the tracking number as both the sort key and the distribution key
An Amazon DynamoDB table with the tracking number as the partition key
An Amazon OpenSearch Service domain with three data nodes

explanation: C is correct. DynamoDB is a fully managed key-value store, and a lookup by partition key returns one item in single-digit milliseconds at any request rate without the engineer sizing servers. A is wrong because Aurora read replicas require instance sizing, connection management, and index tuning for a workload that uses no SQL features. B is wrong because Redshift is a columnar analytics warehouse tuned for scans across many rows, so single-row lookups are slow and expensive. D is wrong because an OpenSearch Service domain must be sized and managed node by node, and full-text indexing adds nothing to an exact key lookup.

stem: A data engineer uses an Amazon Redshift cluster for reporting. One report must join current order rows that live in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database with three years of archived orders stored as Apache Parquet files in Amazon S3. The engineer must not copy either dataset into the cluster. Which combination of Amazon Redshift features will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Redshift Spectrum external tables over the Parquet files in Amazon S3
The COPY command to load both datasets into local Amazon Redshift tables
A Redshift federated query to the Aurora PostgreSQL database
Amazon Redshift data sharing between two Redshift provisioned clusters
An Amazon Redshift materialized view that is refreshed every hour

explanation: A is correct. Redshift Spectrum defines external tables over the Parquet files so the cluster reads them directly from Amazon S3 without loading them. C is correct. A federated query reads live rows from the Aurora PostgreSQL database inside the same SQL statement. B is wrong because COPY physically loads both datasets into cluster storage, which the requirement forbids. D is wrong because data sharing exchanges data between Redshift warehouses and cannot reach Amazon S3 files or an Aurora database. E is wrong because a materialized view stores a physical copy of the results in the cluster and still needs Spectrum or a federated query to reach the two sources.

stem: A BI dashboard runs the same aggregation query against a 5 TB Amazon Redshift fact table many times each hour. The table receives new rows every few minutes. Dashboard latency is too high. The data engineer wants to cut query time while keeping results close to current. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a materialized view for the aggregation, and enable automatic refresh.
Create a scheduled AWS Glue job that writes aggregated results to a new Redshift table every hour.
Enable concurrency scaling on the workload management queue that the dashboard uses.
Create a standard view over the fact table, and grant the dashboard access to the view.

explanation: A is correct. A materialized view stores the precomputed aggregation inside the cluster, so the dashboard reads a small result instead of scanning 5 TB, and automatic refresh keeps it current with no schedule to maintain. B is wrong because a Glue job that recomputes the aggregation is extra code to operate and leaves results up to an hour stale. C is wrong because concurrency scaling adds capacity for queued queries while each query still scans the whole 5 TB table. D is wrong because a standard view stores no data and re-executes the same aggregation on every call.

stem: A company receives daily inventory files from 40 retail partners. The partners can send files only over SFTP with their existing SSH key pairs. The files must land in an Amazon S3 bucket so that an AWS Glue job can process them. The company does not want to manage SFTP servers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Run an SFTP server on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group, and sync files to Amazon S3 with a cron job.
Ask each partner to use the AWS CLI with an IAM user to upload files directly to the S3 bucket.
Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP-enabled server that uses Amazon S3 as its storage backend.
Deploy AWS DataSync agents in each partner data center to copy the files to Amazon S3.

explanation: C is correct. AWS Transfer Family provides a fully managed SFTP endpoint that authenticates partners with their existing SSH keys and writes files straight into the S3 bucket, with no servers to patch or scale. A is wrong because running SFTP on EC2 leaves the company patching, scaling, and monitoring servers, which is the overhead it wants to avoid. B is wrong because the partners can send only over SFTP and cannot switch to the AWS CLI. D is wrong because DataSync requires an agent to be installed and maintained in all 40 partner data centers and does not accept inbound SFTP connections.

stem: Nightly ETL sessions on an Amazon Redshift cluster intermittently hang. A data engineer finds that a session that holds a lock on the target table has been idle inside an open transaction for hours, and other sessions that write to the table are waiting. Which combination of actions will resolve and prevent this problem? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add more compute nodes to the Amazon Redshift cluster to increase the number of slots.
Change the ETL code to COMMIT each transaction as soon as its work completes.
Enable concurrency scaling on the workload management queue that the ETL sessions use.
Query STV_LOCKS to identify the blocking process, and end it with PG_TERMINATE_BACKEND.
Run VACUUM FULL on the target table after every ETL run.

explanation: B is correct. Ending each transaction as soon as its work finishes releases the table lock and prevents an idle session from holding it for hours. D is correct. STV_LOCKS shows which process holds the lock, and PG_TERMINATE_BACKEND ends that session so the waiting writers proceed. A is wrong because a lock wait is a serialization problem rather than a capacity problem, and more nodes do not release a held lock. C is wrong because concurrency scaling routes eligible read queries to extra capacity and does not affect write locks on a table. E is wrong because VACUUM FULL reclaims space and re-sorts rows while taking its own locks, which can make contention worse.

stem: A data engineer runs an ALTER TABLE statement on an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance to add a column. The statement never finishes, and new queries against the table begin to queue. The engineer confirms that a reporting query has been running against the same table for two hours. Which action will let the ALTER TABLE statement complete?

options.text: Increase the DB instance class so that more CPU is available to the ALTER TABLE statement.
Create a read replica of the DB instance, and run the ALTER TABLE statement on the replica.
Find the blocking session in pg_stat_activity, and end it with pg_terminate_backend.
Raise the max_locks_per_transaction parameter value, and reboot the DB instance.

explanation: C is correct. ALTER TABLE needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which conflicts with the ACCESS SHARE lock held by the two-hour reporting query, so the DDL queues and blocks every request behind it; ending the blocking session releases the lock. A is wrong because the statement is waiting on a lock rather than on CPU, so a larger instance class changes nothing. B is wrong because read replicas are read-only and cannot run DDL. D is wrong because max_locks_per_transaction sizes the shared lock table and does not resolve a conflict between two incompatible lock modes.

stem: A company stores Apache Iceberg tables in general purpose Amazon S3 buckets. Streaming writes create many small files, and old snapshots and orphaned data files accumulate, which raises storage cost and slows queries. A data engineer must retire the custom maintenance jobs that handle this today. Which capabilities of Amazon S3 Tables will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Automatic conversion of Iceberg tables to Hive-style partitioned tables
Automatic replication of every table bucket to a second AWS Region
Automatic compaction of small files in each table
Automatic encryption of table data with a customer managed AWS KMS key
Automatic expiration of old table snapshots and removal of unreferenced files

explanation: C is correct. S3 Tables performs continual compaction that rewrites small objects into larger ones, which is exactly the problem that streaming writes create. E is correct. S3 Tables also runs snapshot maintenance, expiring old snapshots and removing data files that no snapshot references, which reclaims the accumulated storage. A is wrong because S3 Tables keeps tables in the Iceberg format and never converts them to a Hive-style layout. B is wrong because replication addresses durability and locality rather than small files or stale snapshots. D is wrong because encryption protects data at rest and does nothing about file size, snapshot count, or storage growth.

stem: An Apache Iceberg table in Amazon S3 is partitioned by month. Query volume has grown, and analysts now filter most queries to a single day. A data engineer must partition new data by day. Rewriting the existing 40 TB of historical files is not acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a new Iceberg table partitioned by day, and use an AWS Glue job to rewrite all existing data into it.
Drop the table from the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and run a crawler so that it detects day-level partitions.
Add a day column to the table, and create a partition index on that column in the AWS Glue Data Catalog.
Use Apache Iceberg partition evolution to set the table partition specification to day granularity.

explanation: D is correct. Iceberg supports partition evolution, so changing the partition specification updates only table metadata; new writes use day granularity while the existing 40 TB keeps the month specification and stays queryable. A is wrong because rewriting 40 TB into a new table is precisely the work the company ruled out. B is wrong because a crawler cannot re-derive Iceberg partitioning, and dropping the table removes the pointer to the Iceberg metadata. C is wrong because a partition index speeds partition lookups for Hive-style tables in the Data Catalog and does not change how an Iceberg table partitions data.

stem: A company runs Apache Kafka on Amazon EC2 instances. Producer and consumer applications use the native Kafka APIs and must not be rewritten. The company wants AWS to manage broker patching, and it must retain 12 months of topic data without adding broker storage. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Migrate the topics to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with 365-day retention.
Migrate the cluster to Amazon MSK Provisioned, and enable tiered storage on the topics.
Keep Kafka on Amazon EC2, and attach larger Amazon EBS volumes to each broker.
Migrate the topics to Amazon SQS queues, and archive older messages to Amazon S3.

explanation: B is correct. Amazon MSK runs Apache Kafka, so the existing applications work unchanged and AWS patches the brokers, and tiered storage keeps older log segments in a low-cost tier so 12 months of retention needs no additional broker volumes. A is wrong because Kinesis Data Streams does not expose the Kafka APIs, so every producer and consumer would have to be rewritten. C is wrong because larger EBS volumes leave the company running and patching its own brokers. D is wrong because Amazon SQS is a queue that removes messages after consumption and offers no topic replay.

stem: A retail company stores order data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Traffic is near zero for most of the month and then spikes more than 30 times during two flash sales whose timing is not known in advance. Provisioned capacity mode causes throttling during the spikes and wasted capacity otherwise. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode.
Keep provisioned mode, and set provisioned capacity to the flash sale peak.
Keep provisioned mode, and purchase reserved capacity that covers the flash sale peak.
Keep provisioned mode, and use application auto scaling with 70% target utilization.

explanation: A is correct. On-demand capacity mode charges per request, so the table costs almost nothing during the idle weeks and absorbs the flash sale spikes immediately without throttling. B is wrong because provisioning for the peak means paying for that capacity every hour of the month. C is wrong because reserved capacity commits to a baseline for one or three years, which is the worst fit for traffic that is near zero most of the time. D is wrong because application auto scaling reacts over minutes through CloudWatch alarms and cannot keep pace with an unannounced 30-fold spike.

stem: A data engineer stores 30 million embeddings in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster that uses the pgvector extension. The vectors are reloaded every hour, so index build time must be short, and the writer instance has limited memory. A small loss of recall is acceptable. Which pgvector index type will meet these requirements?

options.text: An HNSW index, which builds a multi-layer proximity graph over all of the vectors
An IVFFlat index, which builds inverted lists from k-means clusters
A B-tree index on the embedding column
A GIN index on the embedding column

explanation: B is correct. IVFFlat assigns vectors to lists around k-means centroids, so it builds far faster and uses much less memory than a graph index, and its modest recall loss is acceptable here. A is wrong because HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph that takes considerably longer to build and holds more data in memory, which the hourly rebuild and the limited memory cannot absorb. C is wrong because a B-tree orders scalar values and cannot answer an ordering by vector distance. D is wrong because GIN indexes the elements of composite values such as arrays and jsonb and supports no vector distance operators.

stem: A data engineer is writing a design document that compares HNSW indexes with IVF indexes for an approximate nearest neighbor search workload. The team needs an accurate summary of how each index type is built and how each one is searched at query time. Which statements correctly describe these vector index types? (Choose two.)

options.text: HNSW builds a multi-layer graph of neighbor links and searches it from the top layer down.
HNSW returns the exact nearest neighbors for every query.
IVF requires no training or sampling step before vectors can be inserted into a newly created index.
IVF groups vectors into clusters and probes only the clusters nearest to the query vector.
HNSW indexes always use less memory than IVF indexes over the same vectors.

explanation: A is correct. HNSW is a hierarchical navigable small world graph that links each vector to near neighbors across several layers and searches by descending from the sparse top layer to the dense bottom layer. D is correct. IVF builds an inverted file by clustering vectors around centroids and at query time scans only the lists whose centroids are closest to the query vector. B is wrong because HNSW is an approximate index that can miss true nearest neighbors, which is why its recall is tunable. C is wrong because IVF must first learn centroids from a sample of the data before vectors can be assigned to lists. E is wrong because HNSW stores neighbor links for every vector and normally consumes more memory than an IVF index over the same data.

stem: A company runs an Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster on DC2 nodes. Data volume grows by 4 TB each quarter, but query concurrency and CPU use stay flat. The company keeps adding nodes only to gain storage, and cost is rising. Which solution will meet the company's storage needs MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Add more DC2 nodes to the cluster as the data volume grows.
Enable concurrency scaling on the cluster.
Move the cluster to a larger DC2 node type, and enable automatic table optimization.
Resize the cluster to RA3 nodes with Redshift Managed Storage.

explanation: D is correct. RA3 nodes separate compute from storage and use Redshift Managed Storage, which bills for the data held in Amazon S3, so data can grow without buying compute the workload does not need. A is wrong because DC2 nodes couple storage to compute, which is the exact source of the rising cost. B is wrong because concurrency scaling adds query capacity and adds no storage. C is wrong because a larger DC2 node type still ties storage to compute, and automatic table optimization tunes sort and distribution keys rather than storage capacity.

stem: A data engineering team runs transient Amazon EMR clusters that process 20 TB of data each night. Each cluster is terminated when processing finishes. The output data must stay available to Amazon Athena and to the next night's cluster. Which storage configuration will meet these requirements?

options.text: Write output to HDFS on the core nodes, and take an HDFS snapshot before termination.
Write output to the instance store volumes that are attached to the task nodes.
Write output to Amazon S3 through EMRFS.
Write output to the local file system of the primary node, and copy it to an Amazon EBS volume.

explanation: C is correct. EMRFS writes the output to Amazon S3, which persists after the cluster is terminated, is queryable by Athena, and is readable by the next night's cluster. A is wrong because HDFS lives on the core nodes' volumes and is destroyed with the cluster, and an HDFS snapshot is stored inside HDFS itself. B is wrong because instance store volumes are ephemeral and are erased when the instance terminates. D is wrong because the primary node's local file system disappears with the cluster, and Athena cannot query an EBS volume.

stem: A company stores 8 TB of sales history in an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Analysts run aggregation queries that scan hundreds of millions of rows, and the queries take hours. The transactional application that writes orders must keep using a relational OLTP database. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Add read replicas to the RDS for MySQL DB instance, and run the analytics queries on the replicas.
Convert the RDS for MySQL tables to the MyISAM storage engine, and index the aggregation columns.
Enable a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and run the analytics queries on the standby instance.
Load the sales history into Amazon Redshift, and run the analytics queries there.

explanation: D is correct. Redshift is a columnar MPP warehouse built for aggregations over hundreds of millions of rows, and leaving the orders application on RDS for MySQL preserves the OLTP workload. A is wrong because a read replica runs the same row-based MySQL engine and performs the same slow full scans. B is wrong because MyISAM is still a row store, does not shorten a large aggregation scan, and gives up crash-safe transactions. C is wrong because the standby in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment accepts no read traffic and exists only for failover.

stem: A data engineer receives a new dataset of JSON files in Amazon S3. The engineer does not know the column names or the data types. Amazon Athena must be able to query the dataset, and the table definition must be produced without writing DDL by hand. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Run an AWS Glue crawler on the S3 prefix to create the table definition.
Run an AWS Glue DataBrew profile job on the S3 prefix to create the table definition.
Create an Amazon Athena federated query connector that points at the S3 prefix.
Load the files into Amazon Redshift with the COPY command, and query the resulting table.

explanation: A is correct. A Glue crawler samples the JSON files, infers column names and data types, and writes the table definition into the Glue Data Catalog, which Athena reads directly, so no DDL is written manually. B is wrong because a DataBrew profile job produces data quality statistics and does not create a Data Catalog table. C is wrong because Athena reads Amazon S3 natively through the Data Catalog; federated connectors target external sources such as databases and still need a schema. D is wrong because COPY requires a target table definition to already exist and moves the data out of Amazon S3.

stem: An AWS Glue Spark ETL job writes Parquet output to Amazon S3 under a new date partition every hour. Analysts query the data with Amazon Athena, but new partitions do not appear until someone runs a crawler manually. The engineer wants the job itself to register new partitions. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Schedule an AWS Glue crawler to run every hour after the ETL job finishes.
Enable the enableUpdateCatalog option, and set partitionKeys in the Glue job sink configuration.
Add an AWS Lambda function that runs the Athena MSCK REPAIR TABLE statement every hour.
Turn on AWS Glue Data Catalog partition indexes for the table.

explanation: B is correct. Setting enableUpdateCatalog with partitionKeys makes the Glue job write the new partitions into the Data Catalog as part of the same run, so no separate discovery step exists. A is wrong because an hourly crawler is a second scheduled component to operate and pay for, and it must be sequenced behind the job. C is wrong because a Lambda function that runs MSCK REPAIR TABLE is custom code that re-lists the entire prefix every hour. D is wrong because partition indexes speed up filtering over partitions that already exist and never register new ones.

stem: Log files land in Amazon S3 under keys such as s3://logs/2026/08/14/. An Amazon Athena table is partitioned by year, month, and day. After the data engineer runs MSCK REPAIR TABLE, Athena still returns no rows for the new dates. Which action will make the new data queryable?

options.text: Run MSCK REPAIR TABLE again after the AWS Glue Data Catalog cache expires.
Recreate the table with the partition columns declared in a different order.
Run ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION with the partition values and the matching Amazon S3 location.
Convert the log files from JSON to Apache Parquet, and then rerun the MSCK REPAIR TABLE statement.

explanation: C is correct. The keys use a bare 2026/08/14 layout with no partition column names, so each partition must be registered explicitly with ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION that maps the values to the S3 location. A is wrong because MSCK REPAIR TABLE discovers only partitions whose keys use Hive-style key=value naming, so rerunning it finds nothing. B is wrong because the declared order of partition columns does not change how Athena parses S3 keys. D is wrong because the file format has no bearing on partition discovery.

stem: A data engineer runs an AWS Glue crawler on an Amazon S3 prefix that holds daily exports from one application. The exports have slightly different column sets. The crawler creates a separate table for nearly every folder, but the engineer needs one table for the whole prefix. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Add an exclude pattern to the crawler so that it reads only the newest folder.
Change the crawler schema change policy to ignore the change and not update the table.
Create a separate crawler for each daily folder, and configure all of them to write to the same table name.
Set the crawler table grouping policy to create a single schema for each Amazon S3 path.

explanation: D is correct. The table grouping policy that creates a single schema for each Amazon S3 path tells the crawler to combine compatible schemas under one prefix into one table instead of one table per folder. A is wrong because an exclude pattern only narrows what is crawled and still yields separate tables for whatever remains. B is wrong because the schema change policy controls whether an existing table definition is updated, not how folders are grouped into tables. C is wrong because multiple crawlers pointed at the same table name still infer separate schemas and overwrite one another's definitions.

stem: A data engineer creates an AWS Glue connection so that a crawler can catalog tables in an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance in a private subnet. The crawler fails to connect. The engineer must give the Glue elastic network interfaces network access to the database and to Amazon S3. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Attach an internet gateway to the private subnet, and assign public IP addresses to the Glue workers.
Add a self-referencing inbound rule to the security group that the AWS Glue connection uses.
Attach the AWSGlueServiceRole managed policy to the IAM role that the crawler assumes.
Enable enhanced VPC routing on the AWS Glue connection.
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 in the route table of the subnet.

explanation: B is correct. Glue places elastic network interfaces in the subnet, and a self-referencing inbound rule on the connection's security group lets those interfaces reach each other and the database port. E is correct. A private subnet has no route to Amazon S3, so a gateway VPC endpoint must be present in the subnet's route table for Glue to read scripts and write temporary data. A is wrong because an internet gateway would make the subnet public, and Glue elastic network interfaces are not assigned public IP addresses. C is wrong because the managed policy grants Glue API permissions and creates no network path to a private database. D is wrong because enhanced VPC routing is an Amazon Redshift setting and does not exist for Glue connections.

stem: A company runs Apache Hive on Amazon EMR with a metastore hosted on an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift Spectrum must query the same tables, and the company wants to stop administering the metastore database. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Configure Amazon EMR to use the AWS Glue Data Catalog as its Hive metastore.
Deploy an Athena connector for the external Hive metastore, and point Redshift Spectrum at that metastore.
Export the Hive metastore tables to Amazon S3, and query the exported files with Athena.
Replicate the RDS for MySQL metastore to a second DB instance, and point the analytics engines at the replica.

explanation: A is correct. Pointing EMR at the AWS Glue Data Catalog replaces the self-managed metastore with a managed catalog that Athena and Redshift Spectrum already read, so one set of table definitions serves all three engines and no database is administered. B is wrong because it leaves the RDS for MySQL metastore in place to patch, back up, and scale, and it adds a connector to operate. C is wrong because exported metastore rows are files, not a live catalog that query engines can resolve tables against. D is wrong because a replica is another database to administer and is still not a catalog that Athena or Redshift Spectrum can use.

stem: A company wants business users to search for datasets by business terms, see who owns each dataset, and request access through an approval workflow. Technical metadata for the datasets already exists in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Add custom table properties that hold owner names to each AWS Glue Data Catalog table.
Amazon SageMaker Catalog
AWS Lake Formation tag-based access control on every catalog table
An Amazon OpenSearch Service index that contains all catalog table names

explanation: B is correct. Amazon SageMaker Catalog is the business data catalog: it layers business glossary terms, ownership, and other business metadata over technical metadata and provides search plus a subscription request and approval workflow. A is wrong because custom table properties store text but give business users no search portal, no glossary, and no approval flow. C is wrong because Lake Formation tag-based access control enforces permissions and publishes no searchable business catalog or request workflow. D is wrong because an OpenSearch index of table names must be built and maintained and still carries no ownership, glossary, or access request process.

stem: An AWS Glue crawler runs every hour over an Amazon S3 prefix that contains 4 million objects across 10,000 partitions. Only a few new partitions are added each hour, but each crawler run now takes more than an hour, and costs are rising. Which combination of actions will reduce the crawler runtime? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure the crawler to crawl new folders only.
Increase the number of AWS Glue DPUs that are allocated to the crawler.
Add exclude patterns so that the crawler skips temporary files and _SUCCESS files.
Change the crawler schedule to run on demand instead of every hour.
Configure the crawler sample size setting so that it reads every file in each folder.

explanation: A is correct. Crawling new folders only makes the crawler list and classify just the prefixes added since the previous run, which is where nearly all the time goes when 10,000 partitions already exist. C is correct. Exclude patterns stop the crawler from opening temporary and _SUCCESS files, removing millions of pointless object reads. B is wrong because crawler capacity is not configured in DPUs; DPUs apply to Glue ETL jobs. D is wrong because running on demand does not shorten a run and only delays when new partitions appear. E is wrong because reading every file in each folder is the opposite of sampling and lengthens the run.

stem: A company stores application logs in Amazon S3. Each line combines a timestamp, a bracketed severity level, and a free-text message. The built-in AWS Glue classifiers cannot parse the format, so the crawler creates a table with a single string column. The data engineer must have the crawler produce typed columns. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Create a custom CSV classifier that uses a space as the delimiter.
Set the crawler schema change policy to update the table in the data catalog.
Create a custom Grok classifier, and attach it to the crawler.
Convert the logs to Apache Parquet before the crawler runs, and then rerun the crawler.

explanation: C is correct. A custom Grok classifier lets the engineer describe the timestamp, the bracketed severity, and the message with named patterns, so the crawler emits typed columns instead of one string. A is wrong because a CSV classifier splits on a single delimiter and cannot handle a bracketed field followed by free text that itself contains spaces. B is wrong because the schema change policy controls whether an existing table is updated and does not change how records are parsed. D is wrong because writing Parquet requires the schema to be known already, which is the problem being solved.

stem: An AWS Glue crawler runs nightly over a curated Amazon S3 table. An upstream team occasionally writes a file with an incorrect data type, and the crawler changes the column types, which breaks downstream Amazon Athena queries. The engineer must keep the table schema unchanged but still register new partitions. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Delete and recreate the table each night before the crawler runs.
Set the crawler behavior for deleted objects to delete tables and partitions from the data catalog.
Disable the crawler, and have an engineer add each new partition with an ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION statement.
Set the crawler schema change policy to ignore the change and not update the table.

explanation: D is correct. With the schema change policy set to ignore changes, the crawler logs the difference and leaves the existing column types in place while it continues to add newly discovered partitions. A is wrong because deleting and recreating the table each night discards the curated schema and lets the bad types return immediately. B is wrong because that setting governs what happens when the underlying S3 objects disappear and has no effect on column type changes. C is wrong because adding every partition by hand each night is exactly the operational work the crawler exists to eliminate.

stem: An AWS Glue Data Catalog table has 900,000 partitions. Amazon Athena queries that filter on two partition columns spend a long time fetching partition metadata before any data is scanned. The data engineer must reduce this planning time without changing the physical layout of the data. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a partition index on the two partition columns in the AWS Glue Data Catalog.
Run MSCK REPAIR TABLE on the table to rebuild the full partition list.
Increase the Amazon Athena query result reuse window to 60 minutes.
Replace the table with an AWS Glue Data Catalog view that points at the same Amazon S3 location.

explanation: A is correct. A partition index on the filtered columns lets the Data Catalog return only the matching subset of the 900,000 partitions, which removes most of the metadata retrieval time before the scan starts. B is wrong because MSCK REPAIR TABLE discovers partitions and does nothing to accelerate partition lookup. C is wrong because query result reuse returns a cached result for an identical query and does not help a first execution or queries with different filter values. D is wrong because a Data Catalog view changes how the table is presented and indexes no partition metadata.

stem: A data engineer must load a 1 TB gzip-compressed CSV export into an Amazon Redshift cluster that has 8 compute nodes with 16 slices each. The export is currently a single object in Amazon S3, and the COPY command takes several hours. Which change will make the load FASTEST?

options.text: Convert the gzip-compressed CSV object to uncompressed JSON, and rerun the COPY command.
Split the export into many files of similar size, and run one COPY command with a manifest.
Run one COPY command for each table column so that the loads run in parallel.
Increase the number of Redshift compute nodes, and rerun the same COPY command.

explanation: B is correct. A single gzip object cannot be split, so one slice does all the work; splitting the export into many similarly sized files, ideally a multiple of the 128 slices, lets every slice load in parallel, and a manifest names them for a single COPY command. A is wrong because JSON is bulkier and slower to parse than CSV and does nothing about the single-object serialization. C is wrong because COPY loads rows rather than columns, and concurrent COPY commands into one table serialize on the table lock. D is wrong because more nodes add slices that still have only one unit of work to share.

stem: A data engineer must export three years of an Amazon Redshift fact table to Amazon S3 so that Amazon Athena can query it. Athena queries always filter on the sale_date column, and the engineer wants Athena to scan as little data as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Run UNLOAD with the PARQUET and PARTITION BY (sale_date) options.
Run UNLOAD with the default pipe-delimited text output to a single Amazon S3 prefix.
Run UNLOAD with the CSV and GZIP options to a single Amazon S3 prefix.
Run the COPY command to write the table to Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet format.

explanation: A is correct. UNLOAD with the PARQUET option writes columnar files, and PARTITION BY (sale_date) places them under Hive-style sale_date= prefixes, so Athena prunes partitions and reads only the requested dates and columns. B is wrong because pipe-delimited text in one prefix forces Athena to read every row of every file. C is wrong because gzip CSV in a single prefix still offers Athena no partition boundaries and no column pruning. D is wrong because COPY loads data into Redshift from Amazon S3 and cannot export a table.

stem: A company keeps medical images in S3 Standard. Images older than 90 days are retrieved about twice a year, but when a clinician requests one it must be available in milliseconds. Images must remain durable across Availability Zones. The company must lower storage cost for the older images. Which S3 storage class will meet these requirements?

options.text: S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA)

explanation: B is correct. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is built for long-lived data that is accessed a few times a year, returns objects in milliseconds, stores data across multiple Availability Zones, and costs less per gigabyte than S3 Standard-IA. A is wrong because Standard-IA is priced for data accessed roughly monthly and has a higher storage price, so it saves less at two retrievals per year. C is wrong because Glacier Flexible Retrieval requires a restore that takes minutes to hours, which breaks the millisecond requirement. D is wrong because One Zone-IA stores data in a single Availability Zone, which fails the durability requirement.

stem: A data lake in Amazon S3 holds 400 TB of objects. Access patterns are unknown and shift from month to month. The company wants to lower storage cost with no risk of a retrieval delay and without analyzing access logs. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an S3 Lifecycle rule that transitions objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days.
Create an S3 Lifecycle rule that transitions objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 60 days.
Store the objects in the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class.
Analyze S3 server access logs monthly, and move cold objects with S3 Batch Operations.

explanation: C is correct. S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically based on observed usage, its automatic access tiers all return data in milliseconds, and it needs no analysis or rules. A is wrong because a fixed 30-day transition penalizes objects that are still being read, since Standard-IA charges a retrieval fee on every access. B is wrong because Glacier Flexible Retrieval requires a restore that takes minutes to hours, which is the retrieval delay the company will not accept. D is wrong because analyzing logs monthly and running Batch Operations is exactly the manual work the company wants to avoid.

stem: A company must keep audit logs in Amazon S3 for seven years. The logs are queried often during the first 30 days and almost never afterward, and a retrieval time of up to 12 hours is acceptable after that. After seven years the logs must be removed. Which S3 Lifecycle configuration will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Transition objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, and expire objects after 2,555 days.
Transition objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 30 days, and keep the objects indefinitely.
Transition objects to S3 One Zone-IA after 30 days. Expire after 365 days.
Transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days, and expire objects after 2,555 days.

explanation: D is correct. The logs go cold after 30 days, so Deep Archive gives the lowest storage price, its standard retrieval time fits the 12-hour tolerance, and expiration at 2,555 days meets the seven-year removal requirement. A is wrong because Standard-IA costs far more per gigabyte than Deep Archive for data that is essentially never read. B is wrong because Glacier Instant Retrieval costs more than Deep Archive and the rule never deletes the logs, violating the removal requirement. C is wrong because it expires the logs after one year, long before the seven-year retention period ends.

stem: A versioning-enabled Amazon S3 bucket has grown to 90 TB, but the current versions of its objects total only 12 TB. The bucket also holds millions of delete markers left by an application that removes temporary files. A data engineer must cut storage cost by using S3 Lifecycle rules. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add a rule that transitions current object versions to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 day.
Add a rule that expires noncurrent object versions after a set number of days.
Suspend versioning on the bucket, which removes the existing noncurrent versions.
Add a rule that deletes expired object delete markers.
Add a rule that stops incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days.

explanation: B is correct. Expiring noncurrent versions removes the roughly 78 TB of superseded versions that dominate the bucket. D is correct. A rule that deletes expired object delete markers clears the millions of markers left behind when the application deleted temporary objects. A is wrong because it makes the 12 TB of live data slow to retrieve and leaves every noncurrent version in place. C is wrong because suspending versioning stops new versions from being created but preserves all existing noncurrent versions. E is wrong because aborting incomplete multipart uploads is a sound general practice, yet nothing in this scenario points to abandoned uploads as the source of the growth.

stem: An application writes shopping cart items to an Amazon DynamoDB table. Carts must be removed 30 days after they are last updated. The table takes 5,000 writes per second, and the company wants to avoid paying write capacity for the cleanup. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Enable TTL on the table, and store an expiration epoch timestamp attribute on each item.
Run a nightly Scan from an AWS Lambda function that deletes items older than 30 days.
Create a global secondary index on the update date, and delete old items with an AWS Glue job.
Enable point-in-time recovery, and restore the table to a 30-day-old state each night.

explanation: A is correct. DynamoDB TTL removes items automatically once the epoch timestamp in the designated attribute passes, and TTL deletions consume no write capacity units. B is wrong because a nightly Scan reads the entire table and each delete consumes write capacity, which is the cost the company wants to avoid. C is wrong because the index adds storage and write cost, and the Glue deletes still consume write capacity. D is wrong because point-in-time recovery restores to a new table and would discard 30 days of legitimate new carts.

stem: A financial services company must store trade confirmations in Amazon S3 for five years. Regulators require that no user, including the AWS account root user, be able to delete or overwrite the objects before the five years elapse. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a five-year retention period.
Enable S3 Versioning and a five-year Lifecycle expiration rule.
Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a five-year retention period.
Apply a bucket policy that denies the s3:DeleteObject action to all IAM principals.

explanation: C is correct. S3 Object Lock in compliance mode prevents any user, including the root user, from deleting or overwriting an object version until the retention period expires. A is wrong because governance mode can be bypassed by a principal that holds the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission, so early deletion remains possible. B is wrong because a Lifecycle expiration rule deletes objects at the end of the period but does nothing to block a manual deletion before then. D is wrong because a bucket policy can be edited or removed by an administrator or the root user, so it is not an immutable control.

stem: A company stores order data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. A bad deployment recently overwrote thousands of items, and recovery was not possible.
