The company must be able to restore the table to any second within the last 35 days and must also keep a monthly copy of the table for three years. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams, and write every change to Amazon S3 with an AWS Lambda function.
Create a global table replica of the table in a second AWS Region.
Enable point-in-time recovery on the table.
Enable TTL on the table so that old items expire automatically.
Create an on-demand backup of the table every month.

explanation: C is correct. Point-in-time recovery lets the table be restored to any second in the preceding 35 days, which covers the bad deployment. E is correct. An on-demand backup persists until it is explicitly deleted, so a monthly backup satisfies the three-year archive requirement. A is wrong because a stream-to-S3 pipeline is custom code that yields a change log rather than a restorable table image. B is wrong because a global table replicates the bad writes to the second Region within seconds and provides no rollback. D is wrong because TTL deletes items on a schedule and offers no recovery capability at all.

stem: A company runs a production Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster in one AWS Region. The disaster recovery plan requires the company to be able to rebuild the cluster in a second Region if the primary Region becomes unavailable. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Run UNLOAD each night to an Amazon S3 bucket, and replicate the bucket to the second Region.
Create a second Redshift cluster in the other Region, and run the ETL pipeline twice each night.
Enable concurrency scaling on the cluster, and reserve a compute node in the second Region.
Configure cross-Region snapshot copy for the cluster to the second Region.

explanation: D is correct. Cross-Region snapshot copy automatically replicates the cluster's automated and manual snapshots to the second Region, and a cluster can be restored from any of them with no pipeline to build. A is wrong because nightly UNLOAD plus bucket replication yields flat files that must be reloaded into a cluster that also has to be recreated with its schema rebuilt. B is wrong because a standby cluster and a duplicated ETL pipeline double both cost and operational work. C is wrong because concurrency scaling adds query capacity in the same Region and a reserved node is a billing commitment rather than a copy of the data.

stem: A customer exercises the right to erasure. The customer's records sit in a versioning-enabled Amazon S3 bucket. A data engineer deletes the objects, but the records are still readable through earlier object versions. The company must remove the data permanently. Which action will meet this requirement?

options.text: Add an S3 Lifecycle rule that expires the current versions of the affected objects after one day.
Issue delete requests that specify the version ID of every version of each affected object.
Suspend versioning on the bucket, and delete the affected objects again.
Apply a bucket policy that denies the s3:GetObjectVersion action to all principals.

explanation: B is correct. In a versioning-enabled bucket a delete without a version ID only writes a delete marker, so permanent removal requires DELETE requests that name each version ID. A is wrong because expiring current versions creates delete markers and leaves the earlier versions stored and readable. C is wrong because suspending versioning stops new versions from being created but preserves every version that already exists. D is wrong because denying s3:GetObjectVersion blocks reads through IAM while the data remains stored and would be exposed again if the policy changed.

stem: An Amazon Redshift cluster stores a 3 billion row orders fact table and a 400 million row customers table. Reports join the two tables on customer_id, and query plans show heavy data redistribution between compute nodes. Which table design change will reduce this redistribution?

options.text: Set DISTSTYLE ALL on both tables.
Set DISTSTYLE KEY with customer_id as the distribution key on both tables.
Set DISTSTYLE EVEN and a customer_id SORTKEY on both tables.
Create an interleaved sort key on customer_id in both tables.

explanation: B is correct. Distributing both tables on customer_id colocates matching rows on the same slice, so the join executes locally and Redshift stops redistributing rows across nodes. A is wrong because DISTSTYLE ALL copies an entire table to every node, which is impossible for a 3 billion row fact table. C is wrong because EVEN distribution places rows without regard to the join key, which forces the redistribution the plan already shows, and a sort key does not affect data placement. D is wrong because sort keys control the order of rows within a slice and have no influence on which slice holds a row.

stem: A data engineer designs an Amazon Redshift schema. A product dimension table holds 40,000 rows and 12 columns and is joined to several different large fact tables in almost every query. The engineer wants to eliminate the network broadcast of this dimension during joins. Which distribution style should the engineer use for the dimension table?

options.text: EVEN
KEY, with product_id as the distribution key
ALL
AUTO, with product_id as the sort key

explanation: C is correct. DISTSTYLE ALL keeps a full copy of the small 40,000 row dimension on every node, so any fact table joins it locally with no broadcast, and replicating so few rows costs almost nothing. A is wrong because EVEN spreads the dimension rows across slices, so Redshift must redistribute or broadcast rows for every join. B is wrong because a table has only one distribution key, so distributing on product_id colocates the join with at most one of the several fact tables. D is wrong because a sort key orders rows within a slice and does nothing to prevent a broadcast.

stem: An Amazon Redshift fact table holds five years of events. Nearly every query filters on the event_time column for a range of a few days. Scans currently read most of the blocks in the table. Which change will reduce the number of blocks scanned?

options.text: Define event_time as the sort key of the table.
Define event_time as the distribution key of the table.
Create a secondary index on the event_time column.
Change the compression encoding of the event_time column to RAW to speed up reads.

explanation: A is correct. A sort key stores rows in event_time order and records the minimum and maximum value of each block in the zone map, so Redshift skips every block outside the requested date range. B is wrong because the distribution key decides which slice holds a row and neither orders data within a slice nor enables block skipping. C is wrong because Amazon Redshift does not support secondary indexes. D is wrong because RAW encoding removes compression, which increases the number of blocks that must be read.

stem: An Amazon DynamoDB table stores IoT readings. The partition key is device_type, and only six device types exist. The sort key is the reading timestamp. The application reports throttling even though the table has ample provisioned capacity in total. Which schema change will resolve the throttling?

options.text: Change the sort key to device_id instead of the timestamp.
Add a local secondary index on the reading timestamp.
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode without changing the keys.
Change the partition key to device_id, which has millions of distinct values.

explanation: D is correct. DynamoDB spreads throughput across partitions by partition key value, so six values concentrate all traffic on a few partitions; a high-cardinality device_id distributes both items and request rate evenly. A is wrong because the sort key orders items inside a partition and does not change which partition receives the traffic. B is wrong because a local secondary index shares the base table partition key and inherits the same skew. C is wrong because on-demand mode still enforces per-partition throughput limits, so a hot partition key keeps throttling.

stem: An existing Amazon DynamoDB table uses order_id as the partition key. A new report must retrieve all orders for a given customer_id, which is a non-key attribute. The report must not read the entire table, and the production table cannot be recreated. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a local secondary index that uses customer_id as its sort key.
Create a global secondary index that uses customer_id as its partition key.
Run a Scan operation with a filter expression on the customer_id attribute.
Add customer_id to the primary key as a sort key.

explanation: B is correct. A global secondary index can be added to a live table and, with customer_id as its partition key, lets the report query only the items belonging to one customer. A is wrong because local secondary indexes can be created only when the table is created and must reuse the table's order_id partition key. C is wrong because a Scan reads every item in the table before the filter is applied, which the requirement explicitly forbids. D is wrong because the primary key of an existing DynamoDB table cannot be changed.

stem: A company migrates a 4 TB Oracle data warehouse to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. Stored procedures, views, and data types must be converted to PostgreSQL equivalents, and the data engineer needs an assessment report that lists the objects that cannot be converted automatically. Which AWS service will meet these requirements?

options.text: AWS Database Migration Service Schema Conversion
AWS Glue Schema Registry
AWS Glue crawlers with a custom classifier
Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL

explanation: A is correct. AWS DMS Schema Conversion converts Oracle tables, views, data types, and procedural code to PostgreSQL and produces an assessment report that lists objects requiring manual work. B is wrong because the Glue Schema Registry validates streaming record schemas such as Avro and converts no database DDL or procedural code. C is wrong because crawlers infer schemas from files to populate a catalog and cannot translate Oracle PL/SQL. D is wrong because Babelfish gives Aurora PostgreSQL Microsoft SQL Server wire protocol and T-SQL compatibility, which does not apply to an Oracle source.

stem: A data science team must show auditors which datasets, processing jobs, and model versions produced each deployed model in Amazon SageMaker AI. The team wants these relationships captured automatically instead of maintained in a spreadsheet. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events, and query the logs with Amazon Athena.
Tag every Amazon S3 object with the model version that consumed it.
Use Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking to record and query the lineage entities.
Write lineage records to an Amazon DynamoDB table from each step.

explanation: C is correct. SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking automatically records lineage entities such as artifacts, actions, and associations across datasets, processing and training jobs, and model versions, and the graph can be queried directly for auditors. A is wrong because CloudTrail records API calls, so the team would still have to reconstruct the relationships between datasets and models. B is wrong because object tags describe individual files and capture no relationship to jobs or model versions. D is wrong because a custom DynamoDB lineage store is code that must be written and maintained in every pipeline step.

stem: A data lake table in Amazon S3 is partitioned by customer_id, which has 2 million distinct values, and each partition holds only a few kilobytes. Amazon Athena queries that filter on a date range are slow, and the AWS Glue Data Catalog holds millions of partitions. Which change will improve query performance?

options.text: Add a second partition column for event date beneath customer_id.
Increase the number of files written to each customer_id partition daily.
Convert the table to a single unpartitioned CSV file in Amazon S3.
Repartition the table by event date, and keep customer_id as a regular column.

explanation: D is correct. Partitioning on a 2 million value column creates millions of tiny partitions and files, so listing and planning dominate runtime; partitioning by event date matches the query filter, produces a manageable partition count, and keeps customer_id available as an ordinary column. A is wrong because nesting date under customer_id multiplies the partition count further, so retrieving partition metadata still dominates query planning. B is wrong because writing more files into each tiny partition worsens the small file problem. C is wrong because an unpartitioned CSV file removes all pruning and columnar benefits, so every query scans everything.

stem: An upstream team will add two optional columns to an Apache Iceberg table in Amazon S3 that Amazon Athena queries. Existing dashboards must keep working against the current columns, and no historical data files may be rewritten. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Run ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS on the Iceberg table.
Create a new Iceberg table that has the added columns, and copy all data into it.
Delete the table from the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and run a crawler to recreate it.
Convert the table to Hive-style Parquet, and rerun an AWS Glue crawler over it.

explanation: A is correct. Iceberg tracks columns by ID, so adding columns changes only table metadata; existing files are untouched and return NULL for the new columns, and current dashboard queries continue to work. B is wrong because copying all data into a new table rewrites the historical files, which is prohibited. C is wrong because dropping the table removes the pointer to the Iceberg metadata, and crawlers do not regenerate Iceberg table state. D is wrong because converting to Hive-style Parquet rewrites every file and abandons the schema evolution guarantees Iceberg provides.

stem: A company wants an internal assistant to answer questions from 60,000 PDF policy documents stored in Amazon S3. The team must split the documents into chunks, generate embeddings, and store them in a vector index without writing custom ingestion code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Train a custom embedding model in Amazon SageMaker AI, and write the vectors to Amazon DynamoDB.
Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base over the Amazon S3 bucket.
Load the PDF text into an Amazon Redshift table, and compare rows with SQL string functions.
Index the PDFs in Amazon OpenSearch Service with a standard text analyzer.

explanation: B is correct. An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base ingests the documents from the S3 bucket, chunks them, calls a managed embeddings model, and writes the vectors into a vector index, so the team writes no ingestion code. A is wrong because training an embedding model and building a vector store on DynamoDB is substantial custom work, and DynamoDB has no similarity search. C is wrong because SQL string functions perform lexical matching and cannot measure semantic similarity between embeddings. D is wrong because a standard text analyzer supports keyword search, so semantically related passages that share no keywords are not retrieved.

stem: A data engineer stores 90 TB of uncompressed JSON event data in a single Amazon S3 prefix. Amazon Athena queries usually read 3 of the 40 columns and always filter on an event date. Athena costs are high because every query scans the whole dataset. Which combination of changes will reduce the data scanned per query? (Choose two.)

options.text: Convert the data to Apache Parquet with Snappy compression.
Change the storage class of the objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access.
Combine the files into a smaller number of larger JSON objects.
Partition the data in Amazon S3 by event date.
Create an AWS Glue Data Catalog view over the JSON table.

explanation: A is correct. Parquet is columnar, so Athena reads only the 3 requested columns, and Snappy compression further reduces the bytes read. D is correct. Partitioning by event date lets Athena prune to the partitions that match the filter instead of reading the whole prefix. B is wrong because the storage class changes the price per gigabyte stored and has no effect on the bytes a query scans. C is wrong because merging JSON files lowers per-file overhead while every query still reads all 40 columns of all the data. E is wrong because a Data Catalog view rewrites the query against the same JSON files and scans the same bytes.

stem: An Amazon Redshift fact table was created without column encodings, and 30% of its rows have been deleted and reloaded over the past year. Disk use is high and scans are slow. A data engineer must shrink the storage footprint of the table and improve scan performance. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add compute nodes to the cluster so that each node has to store less of the data.
Run ANALYZE COMPRESSION on the table, and recreate it with the recommended column encodings.
Enable concurrency scaling on the queue that runs the reporting queries.
Change the distribution style of the table to EVEN.
Run VACUUM on the table to reclaim deleted space and restore the sort order.

explanation: B is correct. ANALYZE COMPRESSION recommends an encoding for each column, and recreating the table with those encodings shrinks the on-disk footprint so scans read far fewer blocks. E is correct. VACUUM reclaims the space still held by rows deleted during the reloads and restores the sort order so zone maps can skip blocks again. A is wrong because more nodes buy capacity instead of removing unreclaimed space and missing compression. C is wrong because concurrency scaling adds query slots and does not change how much data each query reads. D is wrong because EVEN distribution only changes how rows spread across slices and neither compresses columns nor reclaims deleted space.

stem: A data engineer must orchestrate a nightly pipeline that runs an AWS Lambda function, then two AWS Glue jobs in parallel, then an Amazon Athena query. The pipeline must branch to a notification path if any step fails. The team has no Apache Airflow experience. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Glue workflows to run the Lambda function, the Glue jobs, and the Athena query.
Use Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) to run one DAG for the pipeline.
Use an AWS Step Functions state machine with a Parallel state for the Glue jobs.
Use an Amazon EventBridge rule for each step to invoke the next step.

explanation: C is correct. Step Functions is a serverless orchestrator with native optimized integrations for Lambda, Glue, and Athena, a Parallel state for concurrent branches, and Catch-based error routing, so no servers or Airflow skills are needed. A is wrong because Glue workflows can only chain Glue crawlers, jobs, and triggers; they cannot invoke a Lambda function or an Athena query directly. B is wrong because MWAA requires the team to learn Airflow and to pay for an always-on environment with workers and a scheduler. D is wrong because EventBridge rules only react to events; chaining them gives no built-in state, no parallel join, and no failure branch.

stem: A data engineer orchestrates an ETL pipeline with an AWS Step Functions state machine. A task state that starts an AWS Glue job intermittently fails because of throttling. The engineer must make the state machine retry the failed task automatically and must route unrecoverable failures to an alerting state. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add a Wait state before the Glue task state so that the workflow pauses between consecutive pipeline runs.
Increase the TimeoutSeconds value of the Glue task state to allow the job more time.
Add a Retry field to the Glue task state that sets IntervalSeconds, MaxAttempts, and BackoffRate.
Change the state machine type from Standard to Express so that the workflow restarts faster.
Add a Catch field to the Glue task state that transitions to an Amazon SNS publish state.

explanation: C is correct. A Retry field on the task state re-attempts the Glue call with exponential backoff, which is the standard remedy for transient throttling errors. E is correct. A Catch field routes an error that survives all retries to a designated state, so the workflow can publish an alert instead of failing silently. A is wrong because a Wait state only delays the start of work and does nothing when a call is throttled. B is wrong because throttling errors are returned immediately by the Glue API; a longer timeout never converts a throttled call into a successful one. D is wrong because Express workflows have at-most-once or at-least-once semantics and a 5-minute limit; the workflow type does not add retry or error-catch behavior.

stem: A data engineer adds a DAG to an Amazon MWAA environment. The DAG fails to load, and the scheduler log shows a ModuleNotFoundError for a third-party Python library. The engineer must make the library available to the Airflow workers and scheduler. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Run a pip install command for the library from the Apache Airflow web server UI.
Add the library to plugins.zip in the environment's S3 bucket. Restart the scheduler.
Copy the library files into the dags folder in the environment's Amazon S3 bucket.
Add the library to requirements.txt in the S3 bucket. Update the environment to the new version.

explanation: D is correct. MWAA installs Python dependencies from a requirements.txt object in the environment's S3 bucket, and the environment must be updated to point at the new object version before workers and the scheduler pick up the change. A is wrong because the MWAA web server is managed and offers no shell, so pip cannot be run there. B is wrong because plugins.zip is for custom Airflow operators, hooks, and providers, not for installing PyPI packages with their dependencies. C is wrong because the dags folder is only parsed for DAG definitions; files placed there are not installed onto the Python path of the workers.

stem: A data engineer writes an AWS Lambda function that uses the AWS SDK to run an Amazon Athena query and then process the rows. The function calls StartQueryExecution and immediately calls GetQueryResults. The call fails with an error that states the query has not finished. The engineer must make the function retrieve the rows reliably. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Call GetQueryExecution instead of GetQueryResults to return the result rows.
Poll GetQueryExecution until the query state is SUCCEEDED. Then call GetQueryResults.
Increase the Lambda function timeout value, and then call GetQueryResults a second time.
Set the ResultReuseConfiguration parameter in the StartQueryExecution call.

explanation: B is correct. StartQueryExecution is asynchronous and returns only a query execution ID, so the caller must poll GetQueryExecution until Status.State is SUCCEEDED before GetQueryResults can return rows. A is wrong because GetQueryExecution returns query status and statistics, not the result rows. C is wrong because a longer function timeout without a state check still leaves the second call racing the query; there is no guarantee the query has finished. D is wrong because ResultReuseConfiguration only lets Athena reuse a previous result within a maximum age; it does not make a running query return results synchronously.

stem: A retail company must enrich its sales analytics with a commercial demographics dataset that a data provider updates every month. The company wants the newest revision to land in an Amazon S3 bucket automatically each month. The company does not want to build or maintain any ingestion code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Ask the provider to upload each monthly file to an S3 bucket that the company owns.
Build an AWS Lambda function that downloads the file from the provider's API each month.
Subscribe to the dataset in AWS Data Exchange. Enable automatic export of new revisions to Amazon S3.
Create an AWS Glue crawler that reads the provider's public website into Amazon S3.

explanation: C is correct. AWS Data Exchange manages the subscription and entitlement to third-party data, and the auto-export job option copies each new revision into a designated S3 bucket without any custom code. A is wrong because it depends on a manual process at the provider and requires the company to grant and manage cross-account write access. B is wrong because the company must write, monitor, and update the download code whenever the provider changes credentials or the API contract. D is wrong because a Glue crawler infers schemas from data stores such as S3 or JDBC sources; it cannot scrape a website.

stem: An analytics team runs the same expensive aggregation query over a 3 TB fact table in an Amazon Redshift cluster every time a dashboard loads. The underlying table is updated hourly. The team wants dashboard queries to return in seconds without changing the dashboard SQL. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Create a materialized view with AUTO REFRESH YES for the aggregation.
Create a standard view that contains the aggregation query.
Enable concurrency scaling on the queue that runs the dashboard queries.
Create an hourly AWS Glue job that writes the aggregation to a new table.

explanation: A is correct. A materialized view stores the precomputed aggregate, AUTO REFRESH keeps it current as the base table changes, and Redshift automatic query rewriting can redirect the existing dashboard SQL to the materialized view. B is wrong because a standard view is only a stored statement; the full 3 TB aggregation runs on every dashboard load. C is wrong because concurrency scaling adds capacity for queued queries but does not reduce the work that a single expensive query performs. D is wrong because it adds a Glue job to build and monitor, and the dashboard SQL would have to be changed to read the new table.

stem: An AWS Glue Spark job reads a raw Amazon S3 prefix each hour and writes transformed data to a curated prefix. New files are added to the raw prefix continuously. The job currently reprocesses every file on each run, and the runtime keeps increasing. The engineer must process only new files. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Move processed files to an archive prefix after each run.
Enable job bookmarks in the AWS Glue job properties.
Add a filter on file modification time in the job script.
Configure the job to use the FLEX execution class.

explanation: B is correct. Glue job bookmarks persist state about the S3 objects that a job has already processed, so each run reads only newly arrived files with no code changes. A is wrong because moving files adds a copy-and-delete step, breaks any other consumer of the raw prefix, and must be built and maintained. C is wrong because the script must then track and store the last watermark itself, and clock or late-arrival issues can drop files. D is wrong because the FLEX execution class only changes how capacity is billed and scheduled; the job still reads every file.

stem: A marketing team receives weekly CSV files in Amazon S3. Before the files are loaded into a data warehouse, the team must standardize date formats, remove duplicate rows, and split a full-name column into two columns. The team members are business analysts who do not write code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Write an AWS Glue Spark script that applies the transformations to each file.
Load the files into Amazon Redshift. Run SQL to clean them.
Use an Amazon Athena CTAS query to apply the transformations to each file.
Build an AWS Glue DataBrew recipe, and run a DataBrew recipe job weekly.

explanation: D is correct. DataBrew provides a visual, no-code interface with built-in transformations for date formatting, duplicate removal, and column splitting, and a recipe job can be scheduled to run weekly. A is wrong because writing and maintaining a Spark script requires programming skills the analysts do not have. B is wrong because it requires SQL authoring plus a warehouse load step before the data is even cleaned. C is wrong because a CTAS statement is still hand-written SQL and produces a new table for every weekly run that must be managed.

stem: A company uses Amazon Athena for an executive dashboard. Ten users open the dashboard through the day, and every page load runs the same three queries against a table that is updated once each night. The company must reduce the amount of data that Athena scans. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Enable query result reuse in the Athena workgroup with a 24-hour maximum age.
Create an Amazon Athena view for each of the three dashboard queries.
Increase the number of Athena workgroups so that queries run in parallel.
Copy the query results to an Amazon S3 bucket, and point the dashboard to those result files.

explanation: A is correct. Query result reuse returns the cached result of an identical previous query within the configured maximum age, so repeated dashboard queries scan no data and are not billed. B is wrong because a view stores the query text; every reference re-executes the underlying scan. C is wrong because workgroups isolate settings and cost controls, and running the same scans in more workgroups scans the same bytes. D is wrong because the company must build and schedule an export process and change the dashboard data source, which is far more effort than a workgroup setting.

stem: A data engineer must prevent unplanned Amazon Athena spending in a shared analytics account. A single ad hoc query must be canceled if it scans more than 1 TB. The team must also be notified when all of the team's queries together scan more than 20 TB in one day. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure a per-query data usage control limit of 1 TB in the workgroup.
Create an AWS Budgets action that stops all Athena queries when the monthly budget for the account is exceeded.
Configure a workgroup data usage control limit of 20 TB per day with an Amazon SNS alert.
Apply an IAM policy that denies the athena:StartQueryExecution action to all analyst roles.
Enable Requester Pays on the Amazon S3 bucket that contains the data that analysts query.

explanation: A is correct. The per-query data usage control in an Athena workgroup cancels any single query that scans more than the configured number of bytes. C is correct. The workgroup-level data usage control aggregates bytes scanned over a time period and triggers an Amazon SNS action when the threshold is crossed. B is wrong because AWS Budgets actions work on cost data that arrives hours later and cannot cancel an individual query at 1 TB. D is wrong because denying StartQueryExecution blocks all analysis rather than limiting expensive queries. E is wrong because Requester Pays shifts S3 request and transfer charges to the reader; Athena scan charges and the two thresholds are unaffected.

stem: A partner uploads small JSON files to an Amazon S3 bucket at unpredictable times. Each file must be validated and written to an Amazon DynamoDB table within one minute of arrival. Files are never larger than 5 MB. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Schedule an AWS Glue job every minute to scan the bucket for new files.
Run an Amazon EMR cluster that polls the bucket and processes new files.
Configure an S3 event notification that invokes an AWS Lambda function.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that runs an AWS Batch job every minute.

explanation: C is correct. An S3 event notification invokes Lambda within seconds of each PutObject, and a 5 MB JSON file is well inside Lambda memory and timeout limits, so no capacity is managed. A is wrong because a Glue job started every minute pays Spark startup time on every run and cannot start more often than the schedule. B is wrong because a long-running EMR cluster is billed continuously and must be patched and monitored for a few megabytes of work. D is wrong because polling with a scheduled Batch job adds container startup latency and job queue and compute environment management.

stem: A SaaS company must run a per-tenant data export at a time that each tenant chooses. The company has 20,000 tenants, and tenants change their export time frequently. Each export invokes the same AWS Lambda function with tenant-specific input. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule with a cron expression for each tenant.
Run a Lambda function every minute that polls a tenant schedule table.
Create an Amazon MWAA environment with one DAG for each tenant's schedule.
Create an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule for each tenant that targets the Lambda function.

explanation: D is correct. EventBridge Scheduler is built for very large numbers of individually managed one-time and recurring schedules, supports per-schedule target input, and schedules can be created, updated, and deleted through an API as tenants change times. A is wrong because EventBridge rules on an event bus have a much lower per-account quota and are not intended to hold 20,000 cron entries. B is wrong because the company must build and operate its own dispatch table, polling logic, and failure handling. C is wrong because MWAA charges for an always-on environment, and 20,000 DAGs would overwhelm the DAG parsing and scheduling loop.

stem: A data engineer must convert 2 TB of raw JSON log files in Amazon S3 into a partitioned Apache Parquet table for Amazon Athena. The engineer wants to run the conversion from Athena itself and register the new table in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Run an Athena INSERT INTO statement into an existing external table that uses JSON.
Run an Athena CREATE TABLE AS SELECT query that sets the format and partitioning.
Run an AWS Glue crawler on the raw prefix, and set a custom classifier to Parquet.
Run an Amazon EMR Spark step that writes Parquet files and updates the catalog.

explanation: B is correct. An Athena CTAS statement writes the query output to S3 in the format and partitioning specified in the WITH clause and registers the resulting table in the Glue Data Catalog in one step. A is wrong because INSERT INTO writes into the existing table's storage format, so the data stays JSON. C is wrong because a crawler only infers schema from files that already exist; a classifier cannot convert JSON files into Parquet. D is wrong because it requires provisioning an EMR cluster and writing Spark code, which is far more effort than a single SQL statement.

stem: A nightly ETL process drops and re-creates a table in Amazon Redshift. Analysts query a view that selects from that table. Every night the view becomes invalid, and the team must re-create it. The team must keep the view usable after each reload. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Create a materialized view on the table, and refresh the view after each load.
Change the ETL process to truncate the table and insert rows instead of dropping it.
Re-create the view by using the WITH NO SCHEMA BINDING clause.
Grant SELECT on the table to the analyst group after each nightly reload.

explanation: C is correct. A late-binding view created WITH NO SCHEMA BINDING is not tied to the underlying object at creation time, so dropping and re-creating the base table leaves the view valid and it resolves at query time. A is wrong because a materialized view is bound to its base objects and is dropped or invalidated when the base table is dropped. B is wrong because rewriting and retesting the ETL process is more effort than a one-time view definition change. D is wrong because the problem is dependency invalidation, not permissions; a new GRANT does not restore a view whose base object was dropped.

stem: An analyst must produce a 7-day rolling average of daily revenue for each store from a table that has one row per store per day. The result must contain one row per store per day together with the rolling value for that day. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Use AVG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY sale_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
Use AVG(revenue) with a GROUP BY clause on store_id and sale_date.
Use AVG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id) with no ORDER BY clause.
Use AVG(revenue) with GROUP BY store_id and a WHERE clause for the last week.

explanation: A is correct. A window function with an ordered frame of the current row and the six preceding rows computes the trailing 7-day average per store while keeping one output row for every input row. B is wrong because grouping by store and date collapses each group to the single day's own value, which is not a rolling average. C is wrong because a window with no ORDER BY and no frame averages every row in the store partition, producing one overall average repeated on each row. D is wrong because it returns a single aggregate row per store for one 7-day window instead of a value for every day.

stem: A reporting team stores monthly sales in an Amazon Redshift table that has one row per product per month. The team must produce a report that has one row for each product and one column for each of the 12 months. The team wants to build the report in a single SQL query. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use the UNPIVOT operator on the month column in the query.
Use a GROUP BY clause on the product column and the month column.
Use a LISTAGG function to combine the monthly values into one column.
Use the PIVOT operator on the month column in the query.

explanation: D is correct. The Redshift PIVOT operator rotates the distinct values of the month column into separate output columns and aggregates sales for each product row. A is wrong because UNPIVOT does the opposite: it converts columns into rows. B is wrong because grouping by product and month keeps 12 rows per product rather than 12 columns. C is wrong because LISTAGG concatenates the values into a single delimited string column, which is not a column per month.

stem: A company builds an Amazon QuickSight dashboard on a 500 GB table in Amazon Redshift. Eight hundred employees open the dashboard each morning, and the resulting queries slow down the cluster. The dashboard data may be up to one day old. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Use a direct query dataset, and add more nodes to the Redshift cluster.
Import the dataset into SPICE, and schedule a daily refresh.
Use a direct query dataset, and enable concurrency scaling on the cluster.
Export the table to Amazon S3 each day, and query the data with Amazon Athena.

explanation: B is correct. SPICE holds an in-memory copy of the dataset, so dashboard views are served by QuickSight instead of Redshift, and a daily refresh satisfies the one-day freshness requirement. A is wrong because resizing the cluster raises cost permanently and every dashboard view still runs a query on Redshift. C is wrong because concurrency scaling adds burst capacity and usage charges but leaves all 800 morning sessions querying the cluster. D is wrong because it requires building and scheduling an export pipeline and rebuilding the dashboard against a new data source.

stem: A data engineer receives a new 40-column dataset in Amazon S3. Before designing transformations, the engineer must learn each column's data type, value distribution, missing-value counts, and correlations. The engineer wants a visual summary and does not want to write code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Create an AWS Glue crawler, and review the table schema in the Data Catalog.
Load the data into Amazon Redshift, and run SQL statements against each column.
Run an AWS Glue DataBrew profile job on the dataset.
Create an Amazon Athena table, and run one aggregation query for each column.

explanation: C is correct. A DataBrew profile job produces a visual profile with per-column data types, value distributions, missing and invalid counts, and a correlation matrix, without any code. A is wrong because a crawler only infers column names and data types; it produces no statistics or distributions. B is wrong because it requires a warehouse load plus 40 hand-written SQL statements and returns no visualizations. D is wrong because writing one aggregation query per column is manual work and still yields raw numbers rather than a profile.

stem: A data scientist wants to explore 5 TB of Apache Parquet data in Amazon S3 interactively by using PySpark and by plotting intermediate results in a notebook. The exploration happens occasionally and unpredictably. The scientist does not want to manage clusters. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use an Amazon Athena notebook that runs on Apache Spark.
Launch a long-running Amazon EMR cluster, and attach a JupyterHub application.
Run PySpark on an Amazon EC2 instance that has Apache Spark installed.
Create an AWS Glue Spark job, and print results to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

explanation: A is correct. Athena notebooks run Apache Spark on serverless capacity inside an Athena Spark-enabled workgroup, so PySpark cells and plots run interactively with no cluster to size, patch, or stop. B is wrong because a long-running EMR cluster is billed continuously and must be administered for work that happens only occasionally. C is wrong because the scientist must install, configure, and patch Spark and size the instance for 5 TB of data. D is wrong because a Glue job is batch oriented; printing to CloudWatch Logs gives no interactive cells and no plots.

stem: A startup runs analytics queries in a provisioned Amazon Redshift cluster. The cluster is idle for about 20 hours each day, but query volume spikes without warning during business hours. The company wants to pay only for the capacity that queries actually consume. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Pause the provisioned cluster each night, and resume the cluster every morning.
Buy a one-year reserved node, and keep the provisioned cluster running.
Resize the provisioned cluster to fewer nodes, and enable concurrency scaling.
Migrate the workload to Amazon Redshift Serverless, and set a maximum RPU limit.

explanation: D is correct. Redshift Serverless bills by RPU-seconds consumed, scales automatically with unpredictable spikes, and pauses itself when no queries run, so there is no capacity to plan. A is wrong because pause and resume must be scheduled and still bills for the entire window the cluster is running, whether or not queries arrive. B is wrong because a reserved node commits to paying for a full year of always-on capacity that is idle 20 hours a day. C is wrong because a smaller cluster still runs and bills continuously, and concurrency scaling adds usage charges on top of the base cluster.

stem: A data science team must explore a tabular dataset in Amazon S3, fix missing values, encode categorical columns, and then reuse the same steps in a repeatable processing job. The team wants a visual interface for building the steps. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Write a pandas script in a self-managed Jupyter notebook that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance.
Use Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler to build a flow and export a job.
Use Amazon Athena SQL statements to apply each transformation to the dataset.
Use Amazon QuickSight calculated fields to apply each transformation to the dataset.

explanation: B is correct. SageMaker Data Wrangler provides a visual flow with built-in transforms for missing values and categorical encoding, and the finished flow can be exported as a repeatable processing job. A is wrong because the team must manage the instance and hand-code every transform, with no visual builder. C is wrong because Athena SQL requires hand-written statements for each transform and is not a visual data preparation tool. D is wrong because QuickSight calculated fields exist only inside an analysis for presentation; they do not produce a reusable processing job.

stem: A company keeps five years of order history as Apache Parquet files in Amazon S3 and keeps the current year of orders in an Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster. Analysts must join the historical files with the Redshift tables in a single query without loading the files into the cluster. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use the COPY command to load all five years of historical Parquet files into the cluster.
Create an Amazon Athena federated query connector that connects to the Redshift cluster.
Run an AWS Glue crawler on the S3 prefix to create Data Catalog tables.
Create an external schema in Redshift that references the Glue Data Catalog database.
Create a Redshift materialized view that reads the Parquet files directly from the S3 bucket.

explanation: C is correct. The historical files must be registered as tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog before Redshift Spectrum can read them, and a crawler infers the schema and partitions automatically. D is correct. An external schema that points at the Glue Data Catalog database exposes those tables to Redshift Spectrum so analysts can join them with local tables in one statement. A is wrong because it loads the data into the cluster, which the requirement forbids and which consumes cluster storage. B is wrong because an Athena federated connector runs the query from Athena, not from the Redshift cluster, and it adds a Lambda connector to operate. E is wrong because a Redshift materialized view can only be defined over tables the cluster can already resolve, so it cannot read raw S3 files without an external schema.

stem: An Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster serves a BI tool. Between 9 AM and 11 AM, dashboard queries wait in the queue while the cluster is fully used. For the rest of the day the cluster is underused. The company must remove the queue wait during the peak. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Add nodes to the cluster before the peak, and remove the nodes afterward.
Move dashboard queries to a second always-on Redshift cluster.
Enable concurrency scaling on the WLM queue that serves the dashboard.
Create a materialized view for every query that the dashboard tool runs.

explanation: C is correct. Concurrency scaling automatically adds transient cluster capacity when queries begin to queue on the configured WLM queue and removes it when the burst ends, which is a single queue setting. A is wrong because scheduled resize operations must be automated and monitored and take time to redistribute data. B is wrong because a second always-on cluster doubles cost and requires the data to be kept in sync. D is wrong because building and refreshing a materialized view for every dashboard query is significant ongoing work and does not help ad hoc queries.

stem: An Amazon Redshift cluster runs long ETL statements and short analyst queries in the same manual WLM queue. During ETL runs, analyst queries wait several minutes. The company must give analyst queries priority over ETL statements without tuning memory and slot counts by hand. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Switch to automatic WLM, and assign query priorities to the query groups.
Increase the number of slots in the manual WLM queue that runs both workloads.
Enable Amazon Redshift Spectrum for the ETL statements that write to Amazon S3.
Create a second manual WLM queue, and give the queue a larger memory percentage.

explanation: A is correct. Automatic WLM lets Redshift manage memory and concurrency dynamically, and query priorities let the analyst query group preempt lower priority ETL work without manual slot tuning. B is wrong because more slots divide the same memory into smaller shares, which can cause disk-based queries and does not prioritize analysts. C is wrong because Redshift Spectrum reads external S3 tables and does not change how local queries are scheduled. D is wrong because a second manual queue is exactly the hand tuning of memory percentages and slots that the requirement excludes.

stem: An AWS Glue Spark job that uses G.1X workers fails with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError in the executors during a large join. The engineer doubled the number of workers, but the job still fails with the same error. The engineer must make the job succeed without changing the transformation logic. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Increase the job timeout value, and then rerun the job with the same configuration.
Change the worker type to G.2X to double the memory for each executor.
Enable job bookmarks so that the job processes fewer input files during each run.
Change the execution class of the job from STANDARD to FLEX to add spare capacity.

explanation: B is correct. An executor OutOfMemoryError that persists after adding workers means individual tasks need more heap, and G.2X provides twice the vCPU and memory per worker compared with G.1X. A is wrong because the job is failing on memory, not running past a time limit, so a longer timeout changes nothing. C is wrong because bookmarks control which files are read on later runs; the first full run still has to join the same large volume. D is wrong because the FLEX execution class only changes how capacity is scheduled and billed; each worker still has the same memory.

stem: A data pipeline uses 12 AWS Lambda functions that write logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. After a failed run, an engineer must find every log entry that contains a specific correlation ID across all 12 log groups and count the errors for each function. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Export the log groups to Amazon S3, and query the objects with Amazon Athena.
Stream the log groups to Amazon OpenSearch Service, and build a search dashboard.
Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query across the 12 log groups.
Download the log streams, and search them with a script on an EC2 instance.

explanation: C is correct. Logs Insights queries multiple log groups in one statement, filters on a field such as a correlation ID, and aggregates counts with stats by, with no data movement. A is wrong because an export task plus table creation must run before any query can be issued, which is slow for a one-time investigation. B is wrong because standing up an OpenSearch domain and delivery pipeline is heavy work for a single ad hoc search. D is wrong because downloading and grepping log streams is manual, slow, and must be repeated for each of the 12 groups.

stem: A company runs 30 AWS Glue jobs each night. The on-call engineer must receive an email within a few minutes whenever any Glue job run fails. The company does not want to poll the AWS Glue API. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function that calls the GetJobRuns API for every job every five minutes.
Create an EventBridge rule that matches Glue Job State Change events with a FAILED state.
Enable Amazon CloudWatch detailed monitoring on the AWS Glue service in the account.
Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the total DPU hours metric for AWS Glue.
Create an Amazon SNS topic with an email subscription as the rule target.

explanation: B is correct. AWS Glue emits a Glue Job State Change event to the default event bus, and an EventBridge rule can match on a FAILED state for any job. E is correct. An Amazon SNS topic with an email subscription set as the rule target delivers the notification to the on-call engineer within moments of the event. A is wrong because polling GetJobRuns is exactly what the company wants to avoid, and it adds up to five minutes of delay. C is wrong because detailed monitoring changes metric granularity and does not produce a failure notification. D is wrong because DPU hours measure consumption; a job can fail without moving that metric past any threshold.

stem: An application writes structured logs to an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group. The operations team must be notified whenever the phrase DataQualityFailure appears more than five times in 15 minutes. The team does not want to run scheduled queries. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a metric filter on the log group. Create an alarm on the metric.
Create a subscription filter that sends matching events to Amazon S3.
Schedule a CloudWatch Logs Insights query, and email the results to the team.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the IncomingLogEvents metric for the log group.

explanation: A is correct. A metric filter converts matching log events into a CloudWatch metric as the events arrive, and an alarm on that metric with a sum threshold of five over 15 minutes notifies an SNS topic. B is wrong because a subscription filter only delivers matching events to a destination; storing them in S3 raises no alarm. C is wrong because the requirement explicitly excludes scheduled queries, and a query run on a schedule detects the condition only at the next run. D is wrong because IncomingLogEvents counts all log events regardless of content, so it cannot isolate the DataQualityFailure phrase.

stem: Objects disappeared from a production Amazon S3 data lake bucket. A review shows that AWS CloudTrail is enabled for management events only. The company must be able to identify the IAM principal that deletes an object in the future and must query one year of that activity. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable CloudTrail data events for the bucket, and deliver them to a trail.
Enable Amazon S3 Versioning on the bucket to record who deleted each object.
Enable CloudTrail Insights events on the trail to detect unusual delete activity.
Turn on Amazon S3 Storage Lens, and review the object count metrics for the bucket daily.
Create an Athena table over the CloudTrail log objects, and query delete events.

explanation: A is correct. Object-level calls such as DeleteObject are CloudTrail data events; they are not captured by management events, so data event logging must be enabled and delivered to a trail. E is correct. A trail writes JSON log files to Amazon S3, and an Athena table over that location lets the company query a year of delete events and the userIdentity of each caller. B is wrong because versioning preserves a delete marker and prior versions but does not record which principal issued the call. C is wrong because Insights events summarize unusual call-rate patterns and do not record individual object deletions. D is wrong because Storage Lens reports aggregated storage metrics and never identifies an API caller.

stem: A data engineer must investigate why a transient Amazon EMR cluster failed. The cluster terminated automatically after the step failed, and the engineer can no longer connect to the primary node. The engineer must be able to review application logs after any future cluster terminates. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Enable termination protection on the cluster so that the cluster stays running.
Specify an Amazon S3 log URI when the cluster is created.
Install the CloudWatch agent on the primary node after the cluster starts.
Enable EMR managed scaling so that at least one core node remains available.

explanation: B is correct. When a log URI is configured at cluster creation, Amazon EMR archives step, instance, and application logs to that Amazon S3 location, so they survive cluster termination and can be read later. A is wrong because keeping clusters running to preserve logs wastes compute and does not help when a cluster has already terminated. C is wrong because the agent must be installed on every node after each cluster launches, and logs written before the agent starts are still lost. D is wrong because managed scaling adjusts capacity for running work; it does not persist logs and does not keep a terminated cluster alive.

stem: A company must give support engineers full-text search and dashboards over application logs that AWS Lambda functions write to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. New log events must be searchable within a few minutes. The company wants a managed delivery path that requires no custom polling code. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an hourly AWS Glue job that copies the log group contents into Amazon OpenSearch Service.
Create a subscription filter on the CloudWatch Logs log group that sends events to a delivery stream.
Export the log group to Amazon S3 every hour, and index the objects with an AWS Lambda function.
Create an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream that has Amazon OpenSearch Service as the destination.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that forwards each log event to Amazon OpenSearch Service.

explanation: B is correct. A CloudWatch Logs subscription filter streams matching log events to a supported destination in near real time without any polling code. D is correct. Amazon Data Firehose accepts the subscribed stream, buffers it, and delivers the records to an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain, where support engineers get full-text search and dashboards. A is wrong because an hourly batch copy breaks the few-minutes freshness requirement and adds a job to maintain. C is wrong because CloudWatch Logs export tasks are batch operations with hourly latency plus custom indexing code. E is wrong because EventBridge does not consume CloudWatch Logs events as a source, and OpenSearch Service is not an EventBridge target.

stem: A company runs nightly Apache Spark jobs on an Amazon EMR cluster that uses fixed On-Demand instance groups. Job input size varies widely, so the cluster is often idle or undersized. The jobs can tolerate the loss of some compute nodes. The company must reduce EMR cost. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use instance fleets, and request Spot Instances for the task nodes.
Run the primary node and all core nodes on Spot Instances to lower the hourly cost.
Increase the size of every instance group so that jobs finish sooner each night.
Enable EMR managed scaling with a minimum and maximum capacity for the cluster.
Store all intermediate shuffle data in HDFS on larger Amazon EBS volumes.

explanation: A is correct. Task nodes hold no HDFS data, so running them on Spot Instances through instance fleets cuts cost sharply, and fleets can draw from several instance types to reduce interruption risk. D is correct. EMR managed scaling adds and removes nodes automatically based on the running workload, so a varying nightly input no longer needs a fixed cluster sized for the worst case. B is wrong because losing a Spot primary node terminates the cluster, and losing core nodes takes HDFS blocks with them. C is wrong because permanently oversizing every group raises cost, which is the opposite of the requirement. E is wrong because larger EBS volumes add storage charges and do not address idle or undersized compute.

stem: A data engineer must add quality checks to a table in the AWS Glue Data Catalog but does not know what the reasonable value ranges and completeness levels are. The engineer wants a starting set of rules that is derived from the data itself. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Write a custom AWS Glue Spark script that computes statistics for each column.
Create an Amazon Athena query that profiles each column, and write the rules by hand.
Create an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard of row counts for the table over time.
Run an AWS Glue Data Quality recommendation task to generate a DQDL ruleset.

explanation: D is correct. A Glue Data Quality recommendation task analyzes the catalog table and emits a starter DQDL ruleset with completeness, uniqueness, and value-range rules that the engineer can then edit. A is wrong because writing and maintaining a statistics script is significant custom work and still leaves rule authoring to the engineer. B is wrong because profiling in SQL and hand-writing every rule is exactly the manual effort the recommendation task removes. C is wrong because a row-count dashboard shows volume trends and produces no column-level rules.

stem: An AWS Glue ETL job loads customer records into a curated Amazon S3 prefix. The job must evaluate a DQDL ruleset on every run, keep passing records in the curated prefix, and write failing records to a separate quarantine prefix. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure the job to stop on the first failed rule so that no records are written.
Add the EvaluateDataQuality transform to the job, and reference the DQDL ruleset.
Schedule a separate AWS Glue Data Quality task to run after the job finishes.
Enable job bookmarks so that failing records are reprocessed on the next job run.
Use the row-level outcomes output of the transform to filter records into two writes.

explanation: B is correct. The EvaluateDataQuality transform runs a DQDL ruleset inside the job on every run, so the checks happen while the data is being processed. E is correct. The transform can emit row-level outcomes that flag each record as passed or failed, and the job can branch on that column to write clean rows to the curated prefix and failing rows to a quarantine prefix. A is wrong because stopping the job discards the good records instead of routing only the bad ones. C is wrong because a separate task runs after the curated prefix has already been written, so bad records are published first. D is wrong because job bookmarks track which input files were read; they do not identify or replay individual failing records.

stem: A business team owns a dataset in Amazon S3 and must confirm every week that the email column is at least 98 percent complete and that a status column contains only three approved values. The team wants to define and run these checks without writing code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a DataBrew ruleset, and attach it to a scheduled profile job.
Create an Amazon Athena view that filters rows with invalid values in the columns.
Create an AWS Lambda function that reads each object and validates the two columns.
Create an Amazon QuickSight analysis that charts the values in the two columns.

explanation: A is correct. AWS Glue DataBrew data quality rules are defined visually in a ruleset, attached to a profile job, and evaluated on a schedule, reporting a pass or fail result for thresholds such as 98 percent completeness and an allowed value list. B is wrong because a view only returns rows; it produces no pass or fail validation result and must be inspected manually. C is wrong because it requires writing and maintaining code, which the team excluded. D is wrong because a QuickSight analysis visualizes values but does not evaluate rules or report rule violations.

stem: A company migrated an on-premises PostgreSQL database to Amazon RDS by using AWS DMS with a full load and ongoing replication. Auditors must confirm that every row in the target matches the source while replication continues. The company wants to use a built-in mechanism. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Run row counts on both databases each hour, and compare the results manually.
Export both databases to Amazon S3, and compare the files with an AWS Glue job.
Enable data validation on the AWS DMS task, and review the validation results.
Create an AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset that checks the target table for null values.

explanation: C is correct. AWS DMS data validation compares source and target rows during full load and ongoing replication and records mismatched or missing rows in the awsdms_validation_failures_v1 table with no custom code. A is wrong because matching row counts do not prove that column values agree, and manual comparison is not a built-in mechanism. B is wrong because exporting and diffing both databases with a Glue job is a custom pipeline that must be built and rerun continuously. D is wrong because a Data Quality ruleset evaluates the target dataset in isolation, so it cannot detect that a target row differs from its source row.

stem: A data engineer builds an AWS Glue DataBrew recipe on a 500 GB dataset. The interactive preview shows only the first rows of the first file, and those rows all come from one region. The engineer must develop the recipe against rows that represent the whole dataset. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Split the dataset into one DataBrew dataset for each region in the data.
Change the dataset sampling type to random, and increase the sample size.
Run a DataBrew profile job on the dataset before you author the recipe.
Publish the recipe, and run a recipe job on the full dataset to preview it.

explanation: B is correct. A DataBrew project samples the dataset for the interactive session, and changing the sampling type from first-n rows to random with a larger sample size draws rows from across the dataset. A is wrong because it multiplies the datasets and projects to maintain and still samples the first rows within each one. C is wrong because a profile job reports statistics about the data but does not change the rows shown in the project grid. D is wrong because a recipe job writes output files; it gives no interactive preview and would run the untested recipe over 500 GB.

stem: A data engineer must pull an approximately 1 percent random sample of rows from a 10 billion row Amazon Athena table to prototype a transformation. Every row in the table must have the same independent chance of being selected. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI(1) in the query against the table.
Use a LIMIT clause that returns 100 million rows from the table.
Use TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM(1) in the query against the table.
Query only the most recent partition, and use the rows that it returns.

explanation: A is correct. Bernoulli sampling in Athena evaluates every row independently and selects it with the given probability, which is exactly a uniform random sample of rows. B is wrong because LIMIT returns whatever rows the engine produces first, so the result is arbitrary rather than random and is biased toward the files read first. C is wrong because system sampling selects whole splits, so rows in the same file block are chosen together and rows are not sampled independently. D is wrong because restricting the query to one partition samples a single time slice and excludes every other partition entirely.

stem: An Amazon Redshift table uses a DISTKEY on a country column. Most rows have the same country value. Queries on the table are slow, and one node shows much higher disk usage and CPU than the other nodes. The team must balance the rows across the slices. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Add a SORTKEY on the country column, and run VACUUM on the table.
Enable concurrency scaling so that queries run on additional cluster capacity.
Change the distribution style to KEY on a high-cardinality column such as order_id.
Increase the number of nodes in the cluster to spread the rows across more slices.

explanation: C is correct. Key distribution places rows by a hash of the distribution column, so choosing a high-cardinality column spreads rows evenly across slices and removes the hot node. A is wrong because a sort key controls the ordering of blocks within a slice and has no effect on which slice a row lands on. B is wrong because concurrency scaling adds capacity for queued queries while the underlying skew and its hot slice remain. D is wrong because adding nodes creates more slices, but the hash of a single dominant country value still routes those rows to one slice.

stem: A data engineer defines an AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset for an orders table. The ruleset must fail the evaluation when any row has a missing value in the customer_id column. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Add the rule IsUnique "customer_id" to the ruleset.
Add the rule ColumnLength "customer_id" = 10 to the ruleset.
Add the rule ColumnValues "customer_id" matches "[0-9]+" to the ruleset.
Add the rule IsComplete "customer_id" to the ruleset.

explanation: D is correct. The IsComplete rule type in DQDL asserts that a column contains no null or empty values, so the evaluation fails as soon as one row is missing a customer_id. A is wrong because IsUnique checks for duplicate values and passes when the column is entirely null. B is wrong because ColumnLength constrains the size of the values that are present and does not detect missing values. C is wrong because a ColumnValues regular expression is evaluated against existing values, so null entries are not what the rule measures.

stem: A data engineer creates an AWS Glue connection so that a Glue ETL job can run inside a VPC and read from an Amazon Redshift cluster. The job fails with a connection timeout. The security group that is attached to the Glue connection allows inbound traffic only from the company's corporate CIDR block. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Attach an internet gateway to the VPC, and add a default route to the subnet.
Replace the security group with a network ACL that allows all inbound traffic from the corporate CIDR block.
Add a self-referencing inbound rule to the security group that allows all TCP traffic from the same security group.
Add an outbound rule to the security group that allows all TCP traffic to the corporate CIDR block.

explanation: C is correct. AWS Glue creates elastic network interfaces in the VPC, and the security group on the connection must contain a self-referencing inbound rule for all TCP ports so that those interfaces can communicate with each other and reach the connection target. A is wrong because an internet gateway and a default route provide internet egress, which a Glue connection to a Redshift cluster inside the VPC does not use, and it does not add the missing self-referencing rule. B is wrong because network ACLs are stateless subnet-level filters that cannot satisfy the security group requirement for a Glue connection. D is wrong because an outbound rule to the corporate CIDR block does not permit the interface-to-interface traffic that the Glue job needs.

stem: A data engineer runs Amazon Athena queries from the AWS CLI on an Amazon EC2 instance. The engineer stored a long-lived IAM user access key and secret key in the credentials file on the instance. A new security policy prohibits long-lived credentials on compute resources. The engineer must keep using the AWS CLI on the instance. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Store the access key and secret key in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the AWS CLI to read the keys from Secrets Manager at run time.
Attach an IAM role that has the required Athena permissions to the EC2 instance. Delete the credentials file from the instance.
Create a new IAM user for the instance. Rotate the access keys of that user every 7 days by using an AWS Lambda function.
Move the credentials file to an encrypted Amazon EBS volume. Restrict the file permissions to the operating system user that runs the AWS CLI.

explanation: B is correct. An IAM role attached to the instance supplies temporary credentials through the instance metadata service, and the AWS CLI picks them up automatically, so no long-lived key exists on the instance. A is wrong because Secrets Manager would still store a long-lived access key, and the CLI would need credentials on the instance to read the secret in the first place. C is wrong because a new IAM user still relies on long-lived access keys, which the policy prohibits no matter how often they rotate. D is wrong because an encrypted volume and file permissions protect the key at rest but leave the long-lived credential on the compute resource.

stem: A company stores a data lake in an Amazon S3 bucket. AWS Glue jobs that run in private subnets of a VPC must read the bucket. The company must ensure that the bucket is reachable only from the VPC and that the requests do not traverse the internet. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, and add a security group rule that allows outbound HTTPS traffic to the internet.
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Add a route to the endpoint in each private subnet's route table.
Attach an internet gateway to the VPC, and add a NAT gateway in a public subnet for the private subnets to use.
Add a bucket policy that denies all requests unless the aws:SourceVpce condition key matches the ID of the VPC endpoint.
Add a bucket policy that denies all requests unless the aws:SourceIp condition key matches the private CIDR block of the VPC.

explanation: B is correct. A gateway VPC endpoint keeps Amazon S3 traffic on the AWS network, and it takes effect only when the private subnets' route tables send the S3 prefix list traffic to the endpoint. D is correct. A bucket policy that denies requests unless aws:SourceVpce matches the endpoint ID rejects any request that does not arrive through that endpoint. A is wrong because it sends traffic out to the internet, which contradicts the requirement, and it applies no restriction to the bucket. C is wrong because a NAT gateway sends the S3 traffic over the internet and places no source restriction on the bucket. E is wrong because aws:SourceIp is not evaluated for requests that arrive through a VPC endpoint, so the policy would deny every request.

stem: A company manages the master user password for an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database in AWS Secrets Manager through the Amazon RDS integration. An AWS Glue job retrieves the password at run time. A new compliance rule requires the password to change every 30 days. The data engineering team must not write or maintain any rotation code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that runs every 30 days and invokes an AWS Lambda function to change the database password and update the secret.
Store a second copy of the password in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Update both stores every 30 days by using an AWS CodeBuild project.
Enable versioning on the secret. Configure the Glue job to read the AWSPREVIOUS version of the secret after each manual password change.
Turn on managed rotation for the secret, and set the rotation schedule to 30 days.

explanation: D is correct. Managed rotation applies to secrets that Amazon RDS creates and owns through the master user password integration, and it changes the password on the configured schedule with no customer-authored rotation function, and the Glue job keeps reading the current value from the same secret. A is wrong because it recreates rotation with custom Lambda code that the team must build, secure, and maintain. B is wrong because a second copy of the password duplicates the secret and still needs custom rotation logic in a build project. C is wrong because AWSPREVIOUS returns the superseded password, and secret versioning by itself never changes the password in the database.

stem: A company stores a shared data lake in one Amazon S3 bucket. Twenty teams each need read access to a different prefix in the bucket. The bucket policy has grown close to the maximum policy size, and each new team requires an edit to that single policy. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an S3 access point for each team. Attach an access point policy that grants the team access to its prefix.
Create a separate S3 bucket for each team. Use S3 Replication to copy each prefix into the team's own bucket.
Create an IAM group for each team. Add a condition to the bucket policy that maps each group's ARN to the team's prefix.
Create an S3 Object Lambda access point for each team. Configure the function to filter objects by the team's prefix.

explanation: A is correct. Each S3 access point carries its own policy, so the twenty grants live in twenty small policies instead of one bucket policy that keeps growing toward the size limit, and adding a team means adding an access point. B is wrong because replication creates twenty copies of the data, multiplies storage cost, and adds replication rules to maintain. C is wrong because every new team still adds a statement to the bucket policy, which is the size problem the company needs to solve. D is wrong because S3 Object Lambda access points exist to transform object content during retrieval and add a Lambda function to operate for what is only a prefix-level authorization need.

stem: A company runs a self-managed Apache Kafka cluster on Amazon EC2 instances to ingest streaming data. The data engineering team spends significant time patching brokers, replacing failed nodes, and scaling storage. The company wants to reduce this operational burden but must keep its existing Kafka producer and consumer applications unchanged. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Migrate the streaming data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Rewrite the producers and consumers to use the Kinesis Client Library.
Move the Kafka brokers to larger EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to patch the brokers.
Migrate the cluster to Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka. Point the applications to the MSK bootstrap brokers.
Migrate the streaming data to Amazon Data Firehose. Configure the applications to write records by using the Firehose API.

explanation: C is correct. Amazon MSK is a managed service that runs open-source Apache Kafka, so AWS handles broker patching, node replacement, and storage scaling while the existing producers and consumers keep using the Kafka APIs against the MSK bootstrap brokers. A is wrong because Kinesis Data Streams exposes a different API, which forces the application rewrite that the company wants to avoid. B is wrong because the cluster remains unmanaged; the team still owns broker patching, failure replacement, and storage growth. D is wrong because Amazon Data Firehose is a delivery service with its own API and does not accept Kafka client traffic from unchanged applications.
